    The path of a connection#

    Every client connection string names the region's database hostname, a port, and the project's database:

    postgresql://blog_k2f9_owner:…@db.example.com:6543/blog_k2f9?sslmode=require
    1. DNS and the floating IP. The hostname points at the region's floating IP. Hetzner routes that address to one of two pooler hosts. Without pooler hosts, the PgBouncers run beside xenibase-server, as in the compose bundle.
    2. PgBouncer. :5432 is session mode, for migrations, LISTEN and anything that needs a session. :6543 is transaction mode, for app traffic, with up to 200 prepared statements tracked per connection. Both run the same configuration (deploy/pgbouncer). TLS is required (client_tls_sslmode = require, TLS 1.2 or 1.3).
    3. Who may log in from where. auth_type = hba: PgBouncer reads the generated hba.conf, then checks the password against the SCRAM verifier in the generated userlist.txt. PgBouncer never sees a plaintext password.
    4. Routing by database name. The name in the startup packet picks a line of the generated databases.ini: the backend host and port, the backend database, and pool limits. PgBouncer connects to the backend as the same user and passes SCRAM through.
    5. The backend. One of three things: the shared cluster or dedicated instance that holds the database; the read replicas, for <db>_ro; or, for a paused or archived Free project, the waker.

    There is no SNI routing and no per-project hostname for Postgres. A region has one hostname and one certificate, and the database name alone picks the project. The data API, auth, storage and realtime go through xenibase-edge instead, which does route by hostname.

    The generated files#

    xenibase-server owns three files in the pooler directory (XENIBASE_POOLER_CONFIG_DIR, mounted read-only into each PgBouncer at /etc/pgbouncer/xenibase). Render produces them from a Config of routes, users and restrictions. Entries are sorted, so the same input gives byte-identical files. Names are validated, never escaped, so a bad name upstream cannot inject configuration:

    FileOne line perExample
    databases.iniRoute: the project's database, its V1 alias if it has one, and <db>_ro if it has read replicasblog_k2f9 = host=10.0.0.21 port=5432 dbname=blog_k2f9 pool_size=15 max_db_connections=60
    userlist.txtLogin: owner, read-only login, members' personal logins, probe, edge and request-role logins, logins an owner created with role management, and the static admin user"blog_k2f9_owner" "SCRAM-SHA-256$4096:…"
    hba.confAllowlist rule, then the defaulthost all all 0.0.0.0/0 scram-sha-256

    Manager.Sync builds one Config per region under a Postgres advisory lock, so two servers never interleave. It reads projects in a live status whose organisation is not suspended (PoolerRoutes; a suspended organisation simply loses its routes), their replicas, and every kind of login. A project is routed by its region's poolers, or by the home region's when its region has no pooler hosts. For 30 days after a move it is also routed by its old region's, so old connection strings keep working. A region's files go in the main directory for the home region, regions/<id>/ for the others. Files are written atomically (temp file, fsync, rename, directory fsync) in a fixed order: users, then hba.conf, then routes. A new route is never served before its user can log in, or wider than its allowlist. Then every pooler gets RELOAD (distribute).

    The admin console also carries PAUSE/RESUME around cutovers, KILL for deletes and password rotations, and RECONNECT. Freeze pauses the transaction pooler, falling back to KILL after a wait, and kills on the session pooler, whose clients would otherwise hold PAUSE open. Each command goes only to the poolers that route that database.

    One project's login on another's database#

    PgBouncer has no notion of which login belongs to which route. Any user in userlist.txt may ask for any database in databases.ini, and PgBouncer will open a backend connection as that user. Isolation is the backend's job: every project database has REVOKE ALL … FROM PUBLIC and CONNECT granted to its own roles only (ensureDatabase), so Postgres refuses the login. isocheck verifies that nightly on every cluster. The auth file is also one namespace per region, so login names must be unique across projects. Logins an owner creates must be named <db>_…, may not be one of the project's or Xenibase's own names (platformRole), and lose to a platform login of the same name.

    The per-project IP allowlist#

    New in v4.2.4 (migration 00058). PUT /api/v1/projects/{id}/network stores up to 50 networks in projects.allowed_cidrs. NormalizeAllowedCIDRs turns bare addresses into /32 or /128, unmaps IPv4-in-IPv6, and refuses host bits, zones and /0. A check constraint repeats the limit of 50.

    For each project with a list, renderHBA writes its rules ahead of the default. PgBouncer takes the first line that matches:

    The databases are the project's name, its _ro route and its V1 alias, so neither port nor any route is left open. Both PgBouncers read the same file. The exempt logins (Platform) are the five backend-service logins and the SLA probe. Their passwords never leave Xenibase, and the API keys and row-level security protect what they can do. The dashboard's SQL editor, backups, moves and HA connect to instances directly, not through the poolers. Provisioning and password rotation skip their own connect-through-the-pooler smoke test while a list exists, because it would come from the server's address.

    Risk
    • It covers the poolers only. Instances accept SCRAM logins from XENIBASE_AGENT_DB_ALLOW, which for an agent installed by hand defaults to every private range (the bundle names fixed addresses, and machines Xenibase creates use the cloud private network). Anything there with the password, such as a dedicated project's postgres_fdw, is not subject to the list. The agent cannot tell which private addresses are the platform's, so since 4.2.4 it warns at start when the default is in use, and docs/network-access.md says what to set; the default itself is unchanged, so moves and replication keep working on existing installs.
    Resolved

    The allowlist could be bypassed through an import, which connected from xenibase-server and an agent straight to any address the caller named. An import's source is now checked and pinned, and Xenibase's own addresses are refused. See Nodes and agents.

    Resolved

    The final host all all 0.0.0.0/0 rule also admitted the admin console (database pgbouncer, user xenibase) from the internet, with only its password in the way. renderHBA now starts with host pgbouncer all lines for loopback and the private ranges (DefaultAdminNetworks, or XENIBASE_POOLER_ADMIN_ALLOW), then rejects pgbouncer from anywhere else.

    Resolved

    Nothing checked that the list was enforced: a pooler host still on the pre-4.2.4 pgbouncer.ini (auth_type = scram-sha-256) ignored hba.conf and reported ready. The arbiter now asks both PgBouncers of each host for auth_type (SHOW CONFIG, at most once a minute, EnforcesHBA) and counts a host that is not on hba as not ready, with the reason in Admin → Nodes. It cannot then take the floating IP, and the "pooler host not ready" alert fires. Local poolers raise pooler_allowlist_off.

    Note

    The poolers see the address a connection arrives from. PROXY protocol is not used anywhere: pooler hosts run with host networking behind a floating IP, which keeps the source address. In the compose bundle, Docker's port publishing keeps it for IPv4, but an IPv6 client reached through docker-proxy arrives from the bridge gateway (172.31.250.1) and is refused by any list that does not name that address.

    Pooler hosts, keepalived and the floating IP#

    With pooler hosts (V3 §2.1) each region has two machines. Each runs both PgBouncers and the agent in pooler mode in one container, and keepalived in another, the only one with NET_ADMIN (deploy/pooler-host).

    Getting the files there#

    After writing the files, pushHosts reads each region's bundle. That is its three files plus the TLS pair: the region's own if it has one, else the main directory's (readBundle). It hashes the bundle, advances the region's generation in the metadata database, and sends PUT /v1/pooler/config to each of the region's hosts over the agent's mutual TLS. Then it tells every host the generation, including any that just failed. A push fails only when every host refuses it. A host that missed it knows it is stale.

    The agent accepts only the five known file names, requires the routes and auth file, checks the hash against the content, and refuses an older generation with 409 (two servers raced). It writes users, rules, key, certificate, then routes, and sends SIGHUP to the PgBouncers (apply). The generation served and the generation expected are kept in a state file, so they survive a restart.

    Who holds the address#

    A host is ready when it has a configuration, serves the newest generation the server has announced, and both PgBouncers accept TCP connections (status). keepalived asks the agent's loopback /ready every second. Two failures drop the host out, and unicast VRRP with one-second adverts hands over in about 3 to 4 seconds. Both hosts start as BACKUP with nopreempt, so a host that comes back does not take the address back (keepalived.conf). keepalived's notify posts the new state to the agent, which reports it (setVRRP). The arbiter below moves the floating IP. Only an agent started with XENIBASE_AGENT_ASSIGN_FLOATING_IP=true and a Hetzner token also asks Hetzner itself on MASTER, retrying with backoff for up to two minutes, which keeps failover working while the control plane is down.

    xenibase-server's arbiter checks each region's pair every 3 seconds. It re-pushes to a stale host, at most every 15 seconds, and asks Hetzner where the IP points. Its rule is Decide:

    Following keepalived's MASTER happens at once: that is the failover. Moving the IP away from an unhealthy holder that keepalived has not replaced waits for two checks in a row. Each move, change of holder, split brain, host going stale and recovery is recorded as a pooler event and shown in Admin → Nodes.

    Split brain#

    If the two hosts lose sight of each other but not of Hetzner, both become MASTER. The arbiter reports split_brain and leaves a healthy holder alone, so nothing flaps. (Agents allowed to assign the IP each assign it once; Assign is a no-op when the IP already points at the caller, and the last assignment wins.) Both hosts are stateless and serve the same generation, so whichever receives the traffic routes it correctly. A host that missed a change cannot be ready, so cannot hold the address through keepalived. Two cases remain. If the control plane cannot reach the holder, the arbiter moves the address after six seconds even though clients could still reach it. That is a needless failover, not a wrong one. And while the control plane is down, nothing announces new generations, so a host that missed the last push before the outage still counts as ready.

    Resolved

    Each pooler host used to hold a Hetzner Cloud API token with read and write access (XENIBASE_AGENT_HETZNER_TOKEN), because the agent assigned the floating IP itself, and a Hetzner token cannot be narrowed to one IP: a compromise of an internet-facing pooler host handed over the whole Hetzner project. Now only xenibase-server assigns it, following keepalived's MASTER, and the agent only reports its VRRP state (floatingIP). The trade-off: while the control plane is down the address does not move. XENIBASE_AGENT_ASSIGN_FLOATING_IP=true with a token brings back agent-side assignment for those who prefer that.

    Spec and code differ

    V3 §2.1 says the server "verifies both hashes match". Staleness is decided by generation. The agent checks each bundle's hash against its content, and the server records each host's hash, but nothing compares the two hosts' hashes.

    TLS for the database hostname#

    internal/tlscert keeps server.crt and server.key in the pooler directory for the database hostname (Settings → DB hostname). It has four modes (XENIBASE_POOLER_TLS):

    ModeCertificate
    acme (bundle default)Let's Encrypt or another ACME CA through certmagic, HTTP-01 only. Caddy forwards /.well-known/acme-challenge/ to the server. A self-signed certificate stands in until the first issue, and whenever the hostname is an IP or not a public name (acmeable).
    self-signedP-256, one year, replaced when it has less than 30 days left or no longer names the host.
    filesOperator-supplied PEM files, copied in.
    offNothing is written.

    ensure runs at start, on a hostname change, twice a day, and after a failure with backoff up to an hour. It checks that the pair matches and writes the key before the certificate, then reloads the poolers, which pushes the pair to pooler hosts. Clients are told to use sslmode=require, which encrypts but does not check the certificate. verify-full works when the certificate is from a public CA.

    Resolved

    A region's own pooler hostname (regions.pooler_host, for example db.ng.example.com) used to get no certificate: the server built one tlscert.Manager, for the home hostname, nothing wrote a pair into regions/<id>/, and readBundle fell back to the home pair, so the region's verify-full clients failed on the hostname. tlscert.Regions now runs a Manager per region with its own hostname, in the home one's mode, writing into that region's directory, and follows hostname changes every 30 seconds. In files mode the operator's one pair is still served everywhere, so it must name every region's hostname.

    Risk
    • The hops behind the poolers are not verified by default. PgBouncer connects to backends with server_tls_sslmode = prefer, so it falls back to plain text and never checks a certificate: Xenibase's instances and the waker serve no TLS, so require would refuse every route. That is reasonable on one private network, but not for routes that cross regions: a region without its own poolers is served from the home region, and a moved project is forwarded from its old one for 30 days. Giving instances certificates from a platform CA would let the poolers use verify-full.
    Resolved

    What could be closed of the unverified hops. The edge refuses an XENIBASE_EDGE_POOLER_SSLMODE that could fall back to plain text (prefer and below), and with verify-full and XENIBASE_EDGE_POOLER_ROOT_CERT (poolerURL) it checks the pooler's certificate and hostname against a platform CA, so someone in the path can no longer take over a service login's session. A pooler host renders its pgbouncer.ini at start (PoolerINI) with XENIBASE_POOLER_SERVER_TLS_SSLMODE (prefer, require, verify-ca or verify-full; disable and allow are refused) and _CA_FILE, for backends that have certificates. The default stays prefer until instances do.

    Spec and code differ

    V1 §3.3 has the pooler certificate "obtained via DNS-01 or HTTP-01". The pooler certificate is HTTP-01 only (TLS-ALPN is turned off, and there is no DNS-01 solver in tlscert). DNS-01 exists for the edge's wildcard, outside this package.

    The waker#

    A Free project that sits idle is paused, and later archived (V3 §4.2–§4.3). Its route then points at the waker instead of its cluster, with pool_size and max_db_connections of 1:

    The waker (internal/waker) runs inside xenibase-server on XENIBASE_WAKER_LISTEN. It speaks just enough of the protocol to answer. It declines TLS and GSS, reads the startup packet (at most 10,000 bytes, three tries), and asks freetier.Wake to queue a resume or an unarchive. A request while another operation runs on the project is a no-op. It then closes the connection with a FATAL error that says what is happening (Code):

    ProjectSQLSTATEThe client sees
    Paused08004"…paused for inactivity and is resuming. Retry in about 30 seconds."
    Archived08004"…being restored from its archive. Retry in a few minutes."
    Already active (the route is about to switch back)57P03, which PgBouncer treats as a server starting and holds the client"Retry in a few seconds."
    Unknown database3D000"This database is not available."

    A connection storm is bounded three times. Each PgBouncer opens at most one server connection per paused database. The waker handles at most 256 connections at once, and refuses the rest at accept with 53300, without waking anything. Each connection has a 10-second deadline, and its wake call half of that. The wake itself is one locked row and an idempotent enqueue.

    Resolved

    The waker does not authenticate: it relies on PgBouncer having checked the client's password first. It used to accept any source, so anyone who reached it could wake any paused project, or start an archived project's restore, by sending its database name, and the edge woke a paused project for any request to its hostname before checking the API key. The waker now admits only loopback, its own machine's addresses (the alerts loop probes it), the poolers' own addresses (the local poolers' hosts and every pooler host's private address, from PoolerAddrs) and XENIBASE_WAKER_ALLOW (AllowList), refusing others with 28000 before reading anything. The edge wakes a paused project only for a request carrying one of its live keys, and otherwise answers 503 project_paused.

    xenibase-edge#

    xenibase-edge (cmd/edge) serves each project's backend services at https://<ref>.<domain>. The data API, auth, storage and realtime are described in Part D. This section covers how it connects.

    The configuration feed#

    The edge keeps every project's configuration in memory and gets it from xenibase-server. It long-polls GET /api/v1/edge/config?since=…&wait=25 for changes and reads the whole feed again every minute as a backstop (apply ignores an older version that a resync brings back). An entry carries the pooler database and address, the edge login's and the request roles' passwords, the hashes of live API keys, the JWT verification keys, CORS, rate and cache settings, and the state. disabled removes the project. A project's database pools are kept while its connection details are unchanged, and closed when they change. Until the first full read the edge answers 503.

    Every call from the edge carries Xenibase-Signature, an HMAC-SHA256 over the time, method, request URI and body with the edge's credential or the platform-wide edge secret. The receiver accepts five minutes of clock difference (edgeapi.Verify).

    Resolved

    There used to be one edge secret for the whole platform (XENIBASE_EDGE_SECRET), and the region an edge served was a query parameter the edge chose, empty for all regions, so a regional edge and the cloud-init of every edge node held a key that read every project's service-role password in every region. An edge can now sign with its own credential, xbedge_<id>_<secret>, which names itself in Xenibase-Edge-Credential; the server keeps it sealed in edge_credentials with its region (edgecred.Issue, xenibase-server -issue-edge-credential, and capacity automation for the edge nodes it creates). The server fixes the region from the credential (EdgeScope.Feed): another region is refused, and wakes, auth messages and hooks, storage events and reports are limited to the credential's region. The platform-wide secret now serves only the regions without their own API domain, unless XENIBASE_EDGE_SECRET_ALL_REGIONS (deprecated) restores the old scope.

    From hostname to transaction#

    1. refFromHost takes the HTTP Host, lower-cased, without port or trailing dot. It must be exactly one label in front of XENIBASE_EDGE_DOMAIN. The edge serves a wildcard certificate whatever the SNI says, and the Host header alone picks the project.
    2. authorize looks the apikey up by its SHA-256 among that project's keys only. A key from another project is simply not found, so a Host header cannot be used to point one project's key at another. A secret key means the service role, and is refused from a browser unless the project allows it. A publishable key means anon, or user with a bearer token. The token must verify against that project's own ES256 keys with the project's ref as audience, and carry role: user. Per-IP and per-key limits apply. The client address is the RemoteAddr, or the last X-Forwarded-For entry when the peer is in XENIBASE_EDGE_TRUSTED_PROXIES (clientIP).
    3. WithRequest runs the whole request in one transaction through the transaction pooler, as the role's own login (<db>_anon, _user, _service), with the claims and statement timeout set with set_config(…, true). Nothing outlives the transaction, so transaction pooling is safe, and tenant SQL that resets the role stays that role. Only a feed from a server older than M32, which has no request-role passwords, makes the edge log in as the edge login and SET LOCAL ROLE.

    Pools are small: four connections per login, two for the service and hook roles. They use pgx's exec mode, with no server-side prepared statements kept between transactions (loginPool). GETs that may read from replicas use the <db>_ro route. These logins are the ones exempt from IP allowlists. The Bloom filter in internal/bloom sends a project's counted monthly users to the edge in a few kilobytes. A false positive lets an uncounted user in.

    The schema at a glance#

    110tables after every migration
    73migrations, numbered up to 00086
    46query files for sqlc

    Everything the control plane knows is in one Postgres database, separate from the clusters that hold customers' data: who the users and organisations are, where each project lives, the operations queue, backups, billing, the audit log and the settings. Customer rows never land here, apart from the query texts that query insights and the session reaper keep. Ids are random UUIDs (gen_random_uuid()), times are timestamptz, and money is integer minor units with a currency code.

    Projects, instances and nodes#

    A nodes row is a machine with an agent; an instances row is a Postgres server on it, either the node's shared cluster (one per node) or a dedicated container; a projects row is one database on one instance. The project row is the one the rest of the system reads most:

    ColumnHolds
    db_name, owner_roleOpaque names (p_ plus random letters), unique across the platform. alias_db_name and legacy_* keep V1 names working during the switch.
    scram_verifierThe owner's SCRAM-SHA-256 verifier, written into the poolers' auth file. Never the password.
    org_id, instance_id, tier, regionWho owns it and where it runs.
    statusprovisioning, active, promoting, demoting, moving, upgrading, restoring, deleting, deleted, error. Flows move it under the row lock.
    settingsJSON guardrails: connection limit, pool size, timeouts, disk warning, console read-only, backup retention (ProjectSettings).
    deleted_atProjects are never removed. Every "live" query filters deleted_at IS NULL, so the ON DELETE CASCADE on child tables never fires in practice.
    manage_roles, allowed_cidrsRelease 4.2.4: role management on a dedicated project, and the IP allowlist (at most 50 networks, checked in the table).

    How organisations are kept apart#

    There is no row-level security in the metadata database. The application connects as one role that owns every table, and tenancy is enforced by the API guard (The control plane) and by the queries. Tables that belong to an organisation carry org_id, including child tables where it could be derived (project_members, project_db_users, saved_queries, reaped_sessions, usage_records, audit_log), so a query can scope itself without a join.

    Queries live in internal/store/queries and sqlc turns them into typed Go in internal/store (sqlc.yaml; make generate, and CI fails on a diff). Each query either filters by org_id or says why it may not, in a comment the lint reads:

    TestTenantQueriesAreScoped splits every query file on -- name:, and for each query that reads or writes a tenant table requires either an org_id predicate or a -- tenant: system - <reason> line of more than ten characters. A tenant table is any table the migrations leave with an org_id or project_id column (migratedColumns replays them; TestTenantTablesMatchTheSchema checks the result against a migrated database). A predicate is org_id compared with a parameter, a list or NULL in a WHERE, ON or HAVING clause, or org_id among an INSERT's columns.

    Spec and code differ

    V2 says every sqlc query on a tenant table takes org_id and filters by it, as defence in depth even when the handler has checked (V2 2.6). In the code the opt-out is the common case: about 600 of the 850 queries carry tenant: system, most of them "a project the request already authorized". For those the only check is the guard and the handler.

    Resolved

    The lint was weaker than it read: its list of tenant tables was fixed in the test and predated backend services (project_api_keys, project_jwt_keys, project_services, read_replicas, auth_*, instance_members and others were missing), and any occurrence of org_id passed, including SELECT org_id, SET org_id = … or a join. It now reads the tables from the migrations and requires a real predicate. That caught 25 queries, all of them platform or worker queries on instances, storage_targets, region_early_access, device_auth_requests and the user's own memberships; each now says why in its tenant: system line, and the platform storage-target queries pass on org_id IS NULL.

    The schema ties a child's org_id to its project's. projects has UNIQUE (id, org_id), and the six tables that carry both (project_members, project_db_users, saved_queries, reaped_sessions, editor_preferences, dedicated_requests) have FOREIGN KEY (project_id, org_id) REFERENCES projects (id, org_id) ON UPDATE CASCADE (00068). Nothing checks that a project member belongs to the organisation; the handlers do. audit_log and usage_records keep the organisation of the time and have no key.

    Resolved

    Nothing used to tie a child's org_id to its project's, and orgs.Transfer moved members, logins and saved queries by hand, leaving reaped_sessions, editor_preferences and dedicated_requests under the old organisation. Now the transfer updates the project and the keys carry every child with it (saved-query favourites, which have no project_id, are moved explicitly), and a copy under another organisation is refused. 00068 puts right the rows earlier transfers left behind and adds the keys NOT VALID; 00069 validates them in a transaction of its own. TestTransferMovesEveryChild and TestProjectOrgKeysOnLiveData cover it.

    The operations table#

    operations is the queue described on The control plane: kind, project_id (NULL for platform work), params JSON, status, attempts, run_after, the lease (locked_by, locked_at), the step log as a JSON array, error and timestamps. Two triggers send pg_notify on insert and on changes to status, log or run_after:

    Each log line rewrites the row (log = log || jsonb_build_array(…)). Finished operations are never deleted, but 90 days after one finishes its parameters and step log are replaced by a summary (below), so the TOAST that the logs fill stops growing with the install's age.

    What is sealed, hashed, or in the clear#

    Secrets the control plane must read back are sealed with the master key: AES-256-GCM, a key id in the header so old keys keep working after a rotation, and associated data that names the column and row ("nodes.pg_admin_secret:" + id), so a sealed value copied into another row does not open (Keyring.Encrypt). Secrets it only needs to check are hashed.

    HowColumns
    Sealedusers.totp_secret, users.recovery_codes (sealed hashes), nodes.pg_admin_secret, instances.admin_secret, instances.patroni_secret, storage_targets.credentials, backup_keys.key_enc, project_jwt_keys.private_enc, project_auth_config.providers_enc, auth_message_outbox.message_enc, webhooks.secret_enc, previous_secret_enc, headers_enc, scheduled_jobs.spec_enc, device_auth_requests.sealed_token, auth_challenges.payload, operations.params.secrets (until the operation ends; a rotation's verifiers ride along in it unsealed), and blobs inside settings rows (agent CA and etcd CA keys, platform backup key, SMTP and alert passwords)
    Hashed (SHA-256)sessions.id, api_tokens.token_hash, email_tokens, invitations.token_hash, project_api_keys.key_hash, oauth_clients.client_secret_hash, oauth_codes.code_hash, nodes.registration_token. These are high-entropy tokens, so a fast hash is enough. users.password_hash is argon2id.
    Clear, by designSCRAM verifiers the poolers need in their auth file: projects.scram_verifier, legacy_scram_verifier, probe_verifier, project_services.edge_verifier and login_verifiers, project_db_users.scram_verifier, project_owned_logins.scram_verifier. A verifier cannot be used to log in, but it does let its holder pose as the server, so a copy of the metadata database is sensitive even without the master key.
    Clear, by accidentNone now. A rotate operation's params.verifier and previous_verifier used to be kept forever; they moved into params.secrets, and migration 00062 scrubbed the old ones (The control plane).
    Resolved

    xenibase-server -rotate-master-key used to re-encrypt only some sealed values: it skipped backup_keys.key_enc, instances.patroni_secret, the three sealed webhooks columns, scheduled_jobs.spec_enc, project_auth_config.providers_enc, auth_message_outbox.message_enc, device_auth_requests.sealed_token and the etcd CA key, and its verify step checked only what it had collected, so it reported success and the documented procedure then dropped the key those values needed. rotate now lists every sealed column and settings blob, and TestEveryEncryptIsRotated reads every Encrypt call in the module and fails on associated data rotate does not cover. TestRotateEveryKind seals one value of each kind, rotates, and opens each with the new key alone.

    The audit log and settings#

    audit_log has the actor (user or token, or the system), the organisation and project, the action, target, details, address, user agent and outcome. Migration 00009 makes it append-only with triggers that refuse UPDATE, DELETE and TRUNCATE:

    Resolved

    The migration used to say rows can never be changed "even by xenibase-server itself". The server connects as the role that ran the migrations and owns the table (in the Compose bundle, the metadata database's superuser), so it can ALTER TABLE audit_log DISABLE TRIGGER or drop it. The claim is corrected rather than the gap closed: the migration's comment and the security review now say the triggers stop mistakes and injection through the server's queries, not a compromised server, and TestAuditLogIsAppendOnly pins both halves. A separate migration owner and a runtime role with only SELECT, INSERT on audit_log was not done: there is one database URL, and the split would change every install's roles and its upgrade.

    settings is a key/value table of JSON. Each service owns its keys (db_host, mail, billing, capacity, alerts, backup_key, agent_ca, etcd_ca and others), and secret fields inside are sealed blobs, as V1 §9 asks.

    What is kept, and for how long#

    DataKeptBy
    metric_pointsMinute points 24 h, hourly points 30 daysPruneMetrics, the metrics collector
    query_stats, slow_queries, query_textsRolled up to hours after 24 h, removed after 30 daysPruneQueryInsights
    api_request_logs, edge_reports7 daysbackend services' sweep
    webhook_deliveries7 days; unreplayed dead letters 30SweepDeliveries
    job_runs30 days, at most 1,000 per jobSweepJobRuns
    sessions, auth_challengesUntil idle or absolute expirysweepAuth, every 15 minutes
    operationsParameters and step log 90 days after the operation finishes; then the row stays as a summary, keeping only the instance_id and region that alerts and isolation checks group byPruneRetention, in the tenancy sweep, 500 at a time
    audit_logForever (append-only)nothing
    reaped_sessions30 days, and none of a deleted project after the next sweepPruneRetention, every 5 minutes
    projects and their childrenForever (soft delete)nothing
    Resolved

    When the reaper ends a long statement it records the statement's text (truncated) in reaped_sessions. Statements carry literals, so this is customer data, and it used to be kept with no limit, after the project and even the organisation were deleted (both are soft deletes, so the table's cascade never fires); step logs and parameters in operations were kept the same way. The tenancy sweep now removes reaped sessions after 30 days, like slow queries, and those of a deleted project at the next sweep, and strips finished operations of their parameters and logs after 90 days, keeping the row as a summary. Migration 00070 adds the indexes the sweep needs, built concurrently. TestRetention covers it, and the operations guide lists every retention.

    Release 4.2.4's additions#

    MigrationAdds
    00056regions.api_domain, unique when set, so a region's projects' APIs are served by that region's edge; region_early_access, the organisations that may create projects in a hidden region.
    00057projects.manage_roles and project_owned_logins (project_id, role_name, scram_verifier), with role_name unique across the platform because each region's pooler auth file is one namespace. The check only requires the verifier to start with SCRAM-SHA-256$; the sync checks the rest.
    00058projects.allowed_cidrs text[], at most 50. Canonical form is the API's job (NormalizeAllowedCIDRs); the column does not check it.
    00059read_replicas.hot_standby_feedback, max_standby_delay_s (0 to 900), and when they were last applied or why not.
    00060instances.max_connections, 20 to 5,000, default 100 for existing instances until they are resized.

    How migrations run#

    Migrations are plain SQL files embedded in the binary and applied by goose when the server starts, before it serves anything (store.MigrateTo). A Postgres session advisory lock serializes servers that start together. Each file runs in its own transaction, so a failed migration leaves the previous version. A server refuses to start on a schema newer than the newest migration it carries (refuseNewerSchema), because running there could write rows that break constraints it does not know, and checks again every 30 seconds while it runs. Each file has a Down section, used only by tests that load data at an older version. Rolling back in production means restoring the metadata backup taken before the upgrade.

    A few migrations change data as well as shape: 00010 turns operators into users and moves every V1 project into its owner's personal organisation, 00018 queues an apply_settings for every active shared project, and several add plan limits to quota_plans. sqlc expands SELECT * into named columns at generation time, so adding a column never breaks a running binary's queries.

    The recent migrations are safe to run on a live install. They add columns with constant defaults (no table rewrite) and small indexes, and the tables they touch have one row per project, instance or region. Adding a column with a CHECK still scans the table under an exclusive lock, which is fine at these sizes.

    Resolved

    The newer-schema check used to run only at start, so an older server already running when a newer one migrated kept working on a schema it didn't know, and some migrations removed what older binaries use (00038 renames auth_email_outbox, 00052 drops payment_methods and a billing_accounts column, 00025 drops a column). Now store.SchemaWatcher reads the version every 30 seconds; on a newer schema the server logs it, stops claiming operations (the runner's Paused) and answers /readyz with 503 until it is replaced. It still serves requests that reach it, so the migrations guide now sets the rule for future migrations: expand in one release, contract in the next.

    Part C · Data safety

    Backups, restores and imports

    Logical backups of shared projects, WAL-G for dedicated ones, the encrypted backup format, restore tests, and imports from other Postgres servers.

    Shared projects get a nightly pg_dump, encrypted on the node and streamed to S3. Dedicated projects archive WAL continuously with WAL-G and take a daily base backup, so they can be recovered to any second in their window. Both run as operations (The control plane) carried out by the agent that holds the data (Nodes and agents), so plaintext never passes through xenibase-server. Imports reuse the same machinery.

    • backup3,614 linesLogical backups, restores, the weekly restore test, and metadata self-backups (spec §6.3, §6.5, §11.6), and imports from existing databases (§6.8), through node agents and S3 storage.
    • walg139 linesWhat the control plane and agents share about WAL-G: its encryption key and its environment.
    • backupfmt348 linesXenibase's encrypted backup object format (spec §6.3: backups are encrypted on the client before upload).
    • pgpstream58 linesEncrypts and decrypts backup objects as standard OpenPGP messages (RFC 4880 SEIPD with MDC), so a project's backups open with gpg and its downloaded key alone (V2 s6).
    • pgverify190 linesCompares two databases the way imports and promotions check a copy: per-table row counts and sequence values.
    • pgsource78 linesWhat reading from someone else's Postgres has in common: an import or a Supabase migration copies a source database, and must not change it.

    What a backup is#

    Each backup is a backups row (target, operation, wrapped file key or project key, size, SHA-256 of the encrypted object) and, except for base backups, one object. objectKey names it projects/<id>/<kind>/<time>-<hex>.dump.enc, or .dump.gpg under a project's own key, relative to the target's prefix.

    KindTaken byKept
    logicalThe nightly scheduler, Backup now, suspension, a demotionThe project's retention policy; on platform storage, until the final backup expires once the project is deleted
    finalA project delete (finalBackup)30 days
    safetyAn in-place restore, before it changes anything30 days
    archiveArchiving a paused Free project, verified by a test restore (V3 §4.3)While archived; 30 days after restoring or deletion
    metadataThe metadata self-backup, under metadata/The standard policy
    baseWAL-G, under instances/<id>/wal-g-<hash>/WAL-G's retain FULL n

    A row goes running → succeeded or failed, then deleted. copied marks an original whose copy on another target was verified.

    Scheduling#

    backup.Service.Run ticks every minute on every server. Schedule:

    1. Returns at once without a default storage target or the platform backup key.
    2. Takes pg_try_advisory_xact_lock(hashtext('xenibase_backup_scheduler')), so several servers never queue twice.
    3. Lists due projects. The window opens at XENIBASE_BACKUP_HOUR UTC (default 2); each project is due at a stable offset into it, an FNV hash of its ID modulo XENIBASE_BACKUP_JITTER (default 2 h).
    4. Queues each through EnqueueIfIdleTx, which locks the project, rechecks it is active, and skips it if any operation is pending, so a backup never interleaves with a restore or delete. Shared projects get backup, dedicated ones base_backup.
    5. Queues a storage_switch for any dedicated project archiving somewhere other than where its backups now go, the metadata backup once per window, and the restore test once seven days have passed.

    "Already done" is any backup or base_backup operation since the window opened, whatever its outcome: a nightly backup that fails its three attempts waits for the next night, and the alerts report it. Hourly, Run also deletes backups past their expires_at, fails rows whose operation ended while they were running (SweepStaleBackups) and deletes failed rows' leftover objects. Every five minutes it makes cross-region copies.

    Taking a logical backup#

    runBackup first looks for a backup an earlier attempt of the same operation finished (BackupForOperation), so a retry never takes a second one. dumpTo then resolves the target and sealing (sealing: a fresh file key wrapped by the platform key, or the project key's OpenPGP public key), fails rows an earlier attempt left running, inserts a new row and calls the agent. doDump pipes pg_dump --format=custom through the encrypter and a SHA-256 into a multipart upload, without touching the disk. Last, retention runs over the project's logical backups; its failure is only a warning.

    A failing pg_dump closes the upload's pipe with its error, so the multipart upload aborts; if it already looked complete, the agent deletes the object. An upload the bucket completes after the attempt gave up is caught by cleanFailed, which deletes failed rows' objects before every dump and hourly.

    BackupNow queues the same operation (a base backup on a dedicated project). On a platform target it counts against backup_storage_mb and is refused past it; nightly backups still run.

    Retention and expiry#

    Retention.Expired keeps the newest backup of each of the Daily most recent UTC days that have one, the newest of each of the next Weekly ISO weeks, and always the newest. Counting days that have a backup means failed nights never shorten the history. Policies are standard 7 + 4 (also the metadata backups), and the billed add-ons extended 30 + 12 and long 30 + 52 (V4.1 §4.2).

    applyRetention runs only after a successful backup of the project. deleteObject removes the object, its cross-region copy, and the original a switch copied it from. Final and safety backups carry an expires_at instead, as do a deleted project's nightly and archive backups on platform storage, and deleting an organisation re-dates all of them to 30 days after (ExpireOrgFinalBackups).

    Resolved

    A deleted project's nightly backups used to stay for good: retention runs only in the project's next runBackup, which a deleted project never gets, its logical rows had no expires_at, and runDelete and the organisation sweep touched only the final backup, so up to 11 copies of the database (82 with the long add-on) stayed on platform storage, listed and restorable, against V2 §10.10 and the terms template. Now runDelete soft-deletes the project and, in the same transaction, gives its logical and archive rows on platform targets the final backup's expiry, or 30 days without one (ExpireDeletedProjectBackups); finishing an organisation's deletion re-dates them with its final backups. The hourly expiry now also takes copied originals, so deleteObject removes each object, its cross-region copy and the row. Backups in an organisation's own bucket are left alone. Migration 00075 dates those of projects already deleted, at least a week after the upgrade (TestDeleteExpiresEarlierBackups, TestExpiryRemovesDeletedProjectBackups, TestOrgDeletionExpiresBackups, TestDeletedProjectBackupsMigration).

    Encryption and keys#

    KeyKeptOpens
    Platform backup key (32 bytes)settings.backup_key sealed with the master key, and the operator's downloaded fileEvery .dump.enc, and through a derived OpenPGP key every WAL-G archive without a project key
    Project key (32 bytes)backup_keys.key_enc sealed with the master key, and the file its admin may downloadThe project's .dump.gpg objects and WAL-G archive
    File key, per objectWrapped by the platform key, in the header and backups.key_wrappedOne object

    GenerateKey refuses to replace the platform key, which would orphan every backup. ConfirmKey wants the whole key pasted back, compared in constant time. The control plane unwraps a file key and sends the agent only that.

    The writer holds a full buffer back until more data arrives, so the final chunk is always the one Close writes, and the reader reads a chunk ahead to know which one must carry the final flag (Reader.Read). A cut at a chunk boundary fails on the flag. Each chunk is authenticated before its plaintext is passed on.

    A project key lets an organisation restore with standard tools (V2 §6.3). pgpstream writes plain OpenPGP: SEIPD v1 with MDC, AES-256, no compression. Its integrity check comes at the end, so the agent's restore reports a decryption error even after pg_restore succeeded (doRestore), and the operation rolls back. The OpenPGP keys are never stored: deriveKey feeds 4 KiB of HKDF output as the random source to openpgp.NewEntity, with a fixed creation time, for PGPKey (WAL-G, from the platform key) and ProjectPGPKey. EnableProjectKey creates or rotates a project key (old backups keep theirs); ProjectKeyFile gives a README and the armored private key, behind re-authentication and the audit log.

    Resolved

    Nothing used to pin the derived OpenPGP keys: the key is whatever go-crypto builds from the seeded reader, so a version that read its random source differently, or changed a default in the key packet or its self-signatures, would derive a different key from the same secret, and every WAL-G archive and .dump.gpg object would become unreadable through Xenibase, unnoticed until a restore; TestPGPKeyDeterministicAndUsable only compared two derivations in one build. Now TestDerivedKeysArePinned derives PGPKey and ProjectPGPKey from a fixed secret and compares each fingerprint, armored public key and the armored private key's SHA-256 to constants, so a dependency update that changes the derivation fails the build instead.

    Where backups go#

    PlacementFor picks the project's chosen target (a platform target or its organisation's own bucket), else its region's, else the platform default; a data-residency project only targets marked as in its region. SaveTarget saves a target only after a live write, read, list and delete, never at another live target's endpoint, bucket and prefix, and DeleteTarget refuses one in use, or holding backups unless the loss is accepted.

    • Cross-region copies (V3 §2.5): CopyRegionBackups copies logical backups on platform targets to the region's copy target under the same key, checking the SHA-256 while streaming and again by reading the copy back. Residency projects copy only within their region, and SetResidency deletes copies outside it.
    • Switching target (V2 §6.2): SwitchTarget is immediate on a shared project. A dedicated project gets a storage_switch that points WAL-G at a new prefix, restarts the instance and takes a base backup (reconfigureArchive). copy_existing copies logical backups as twin rows verified by checksum (copyBackup); delete_originals then removes the originals.
    Resolved

    Two targets at one location used to turn "copy, then delete the original" into "delete the only copy": only names were unique, so two rows could name the same endpoint, bucket and prefix (and backups and backups/ give the same keys, Target.Key). Copies keep the object key, so a switch between them with delete_originals overwrote each object with itself, passed the read-back, and deleteOriginal deleted it; turning residency on did the same through deleteCopy when a region's copy target was its primary. Now SaveTarget refuses, with a 409, a target whose Location (endpoint without case, default port or trailing slash; bucket; prefix as Key applies it) is another live target's, naming it only within the same organisation or the platform. For rows saved before, copyBackup and the cross-region copyObject refuse a destination at the source's location (a switch logs and skips such a backup), deleteOriginal deletes an original only once a verified copy is at another location, and deleteCopy leaves a "copy" at the primary's location alone (TestSaveTargetRefusesATakenLocation, TestCopyBetweenTargetsAtOnePlaceIsRefused, TestLocation).

    Restores#

    POST /backups/{id}/restore needs BackupCreate on the backup's organisation. backup.Restore accepts any succeeded project backup; a base backup becomes a recovery to the moment it finished. RestoreInto has the agent pipe the decrypted object into pg_restore --no-owner --no-acl --role=<owner> --single-transaction --exit-on-error as the project's console login, never the superuser, because a dump's functions run during a restore (restoreArgs). Webhook triggers are reset from Xenibase's configuration with an empty outbox (V2 §9.3).

    • Into a new project (the default): a project in the source's organisation, region and residency, created as a restore operation; the source may already be deleted. runRestore recreates the database empty on a retry, restores and publishes. Failure rolls the project back.
    • In place: the project admin role, re-authentication and the project's exact name. The project moves to restoring; a safety backup is taken (once per operation), the pooler KILLs clients while new ones wait, the database is recreated and restored, members' grants are re-applied (SyncMemberRoles), and the route resumes.

    GET /backups/{id}/download (ProjectExport, two at a time per organisation) streams a logical backup decrypted in xenibase-server as a plain pg_dump archive (Export).

    Resolved

    A decryption that failed half-way used to look like a complete file: once DownloadBackup had written a byte, an error was only logged and the handler returned, so Go ended the chunked response cleanly and the client reported a good download of a truncated archive. The runbook's xenibase-agent decrypt … > metadata.dump had the same gap, though it promised a damaged object "fails without writing a partial file", which held only with --out, and its next line restored whatever was written. Now streamDownload logs and audits a mid-stream error and then panics with http.ErrAbortHandler, which chi's Recoverer passes on, so the connection closes without the final chunk and the client sees a failed download; an error before the first byte is still an ordinary error response. The runbook uses --in and --out joined by &&, and it and the project key's README warn that gpg's output is incomplete when it reports an error (TestDownloadFailingMidStreamIsAborted; TestDecrypt now also cuts an object short).

    The weekly restore test#

    runRestoreTest picks a random active, unarchived project with a succeeded logical backup, and verifyRestore restores its newest logical, final or safety backup into xenibase_restore_test_<hex> on the project's own instance, owned by its owner and restored as its console login. It counts every table (TableCounts) and drops the database. Weekly runs alternate between a point-in-time recovery and a logical backup, and the logical runs between a backup's primary object and its cross-region copy (nextRestoreTest); the scheduler passes over a turn with nothing to test. On the point-in-time turn, or when a platform admin runs one now for a dedicated project, runPITRTest picks a random running dedicated project with a base backup, and ScratchPITR recovers it to now as a point-in-time restore would (flush, newest base backup, WAL from the archive, promote), but into a smallest-profile container on the source's node, named by the operation's ID, that no project uses, no pooler routes to and that archives nothing; it then counts every table of the project's database there as the superuser, and destroys the container. It wants twice the instance's databases free on the node, plus 1 GiB. A failure raises the critical restore_test_failed alert.

    Spec and code differ

    V1 §6.5's weekly job restores "the latest backup of a random project"; the logical turns restore a logical, final or safety backup, and every other week a dedicated project's base backup and WAL instead, so a given project's backups are tested only when the draw picks it.

    Resolved

    A dedicated project's archive used to be able to break for months unnoticed: only the flush before a recovery read pg_stat_archiver, no alert covered archiving, and the restore test restored only logical backups, so a failing wal-push (rotated credentials, a full bucket) let WAL pile up in pg_wal while base backups still succeeded, and the first test was the customer's restore. Now the metrics collector samples each dedicated instance's archiver every minute, at the instance's address, which follows an HA leader (collectArchiver: failed attempts, the age of the last archived segment, and the segments waiting in archive_status with the oldest one's age, which is how "stale while there is something to archive" is told from an idle archive), and walArchiveConditions raises the critical wal_archive alert when failed attempts went up in the last 15 minutes or a completed segment has waited longer than that. The restore test recovers a dedicated project's archive every other week (above). Both turn the status page's Backups component to degraded (TestWALArchiveAlert, TestCollectArchiver, TestRestoreTestTurns, TestScheduleSkipsThePITRTurnWithoutADedicatedProject; the recovery itself in the integration suite's TestDedicatedProjectAndPITR).

    WAL-G and point-in-time recovery#

    A dedicated instance runs with archive_command='wal-g wal-push %p' and archive_timeout=60; walg.Env supplies the prefix, credentials, zstd and the derived key. The daily base_backup (dedicated.BaseBackup) runs wal-g backup-push on the leader, then delete retain FULL n --confirm (instances.Backup), where n is 7 or the purchased 14 or 30 (RetainFull). It records a base row and, when WAL-G lists the new backup, forgets the rows it no longer lists:

    Resolved

    One failed listing used to forget every base backup: instances.Backups ran wal-g backup-list … 2>/dev/null || true and returned an empty list, without error, on empty output, so a transient S3 error on the listing after a backup emptied keep and every base row of the archive, the new one included, became deleted, restarting the window the UI shows and PlanPITR accepts at the next night's backup. Now parseBackupList makes a failed listing an error, with WAL-G's stderr, and only "No backups found" an empty archive; the agent's Backup also refuses to report a newest listed backup that started before its push. forgetUnlisted forgets nothing when the listing lacks the backup just taken (an older agent, or a store that lists late), and a listing that fails is a warning in the step log (TestParseBackupList, TestNewBackup, TestBaseBackupReconciliationNeedsTheNewBackup).

    1. Plan. PlanPITR takes the newest base backup finished at or before the target (at most a minute in the future).
    2. Flush. flushWAL commits a transaction with an XID, switches segment, and waits up to two minutes for it to be archived. Recovery to a time ends at the first commit after it and fails without one, so the forced commit guarantees one. A stuck archive answers 409 before anything is created.
    3. Create a new dedicated project on the source's node with its size, version, region and residency, as a restore in mode pitr (runPITR).
    4. Replay. A one-off container runs wal-g backup-fetch, then Postgres recovers with restore_command reading the source's archive (settings in a 0600 file), recovery_target_time and recovery_target_action=promote (instances.restore).
    5. Adopt. adoptRestore waits for promotion, resets the recovery settings, renames the source's database and owner to the new project's, drops the source's console login and resets webhooks.

    The window runs from the oldest recorded base backup to now (PITRWindow). After a switch the previous archive stays restorable from its own prefix and key for the project's window (7, 14 or 30 days), until its base backups expire, and the last takes the prefix with it. See Dedicated instances, HA and moves for WAL-G on a failover.

    Resolved

    A storage or key switch used to cut a 14- or 30-day window to 7 days: reconfigureArchive expired the retired archive's base backups after PITRWindow, a fixed 7 days, whatever pitr_days the project paid for, so from day 8 to day 30 after a switch (which enabling or rotating a project key triggers by itself) the project could recover only to the switch. Now they expire after retiredArchiveKept, the larger of 7 days and the instance's pitr_days (TestRetiredArchiveKeptForThePaidWindow). Archives retired before this keep the 7-day expiry they were given.

    Imports and Supabase migrations#

    An import (V1 §6.8) copies schemas from someone else's Postgres into a new shared project. The source is the tenant's, so Xenibase must neither change it nor trust it.

    1. Preflight. preflight reports the version (refusing 19 and later), size, schemas, extensions against the shared allow-list, and grants and policies naming anon, authenticated or service_role. On a Supabase source the managed schemas (SupabaseManagedSchemas) are left unselected.
    2. Create. Import repeats the preflight and creates the project. The URL travels sealed with the master key in the operation's params.secrets, bound to a random reference (SealOpSecret), which the job runner removes when the operation succeeds or fails and the API never returns; the log and the API see a redacted URL.
    3. Prepare. prepareImportTarget creates what pg_dump -n leaves out: the allowed extensions in their source schema, NOLOGIN stand-ins for the Supabase roles, and auth.uid(), auth.role() and auth.jwt() when auth is not imported.
    4. Copy. The agent pipes pg_dump --no-owner --no-acl --schema=… into pg_restore --role=<owner> as the console login, continuing past failing objects and listing up to 40 (agentsvc.copy).
    5. Verify. verifyImport compares row counts and sequences in the chosen schemas. A missing table fails and rolls back; a differing count is a warning, as the source may be live (decisions M3 #14).

    Every source connection goes through pgsource.Config, which refuses a URL naming any host but its authority (host=, several hosts, a socket directory) and pins Xenibase's connection and the agent's pg_dump to the address the guard approved:

    The guard is outbound.CheckSource: public addresses unless the platform admin allow-listed the host for the organisation; never loopback, link-local, metadata, or a node's or instance's address; and for imports never XENIBASE_OUTBOUND_BLOCK or the cloud private network, allow-listed or not (SourceInternal). The operation checks and pins again when it starts. Xenibase's own sessions run SET default_transaction_read_only = on (ReadOnly), a SET because PgBouncer refuses unknown startup parameters; pg_dump reads in its own read-only snapshot. The Supabase helper (V4 §9, MigrateSupabase) then rewrites policies, copies auth.users with their bcrypt hashes and copies storage, through the same pgsource path, with the credentials sealed in each step's operation the same way.

    Resolved

    With more than one server, imports used to fail at random: the URL was only in the memory of the server that took the request, but any server may claim the operation, and elsewhere runImport failed permanently ("xenibase-server restarted?") and rolled back; with two servers about half of imports and Supabase steps ended so, and a retry after the first attempt always did. Now Import seals the URL with the master key (SealOpSecret, bound to the import's reference) and hands it to provision.Create's Secrets, which puts it in params.secrets beside the password; importSource opens it on whichever server runs the operation. A Supabase step's URL and S3 key travel the same way (sealSecrets, opened in migrationStart). The runner removes them when the operation succeeds or fails, and the API strips params.secrets; the redacted URL stays for display (TestImportSourceReachesAnyServer, TestSupabaseStepSecretsReachAnyServer, TestCreateKeepsExtraSecretsWithThePassword).

    Resolved

    Verification used to read every table in the source, not only the chosen schemas: verifyImport counted the whole source and filtered afterwards, so a login that could read only the imported schema hit "permission denied" on another table and the import rolled back after an hours-long copy (pgverify.Compare had the same shape). Now TableCounts takes the schemas and filters in its catalogue query, and verifyImport and Compare pass theirs; the restore test still counts every table (TestTableCountsReadsOnlyTheChosenSchemas).

    Resolved

    Supabase migrations used to get a weaker address check than imports: services.sourceGuard used the general outbound service, built in main.go with no Internal ranges, so a host allow-listed for an organisation, whose DNS the tenant controls, could resolve into the cloud private network or XENIBASE_OUTBOUND_BLOCK and reach platform services not registered as nodes, which an import refuses. Now sourceGuard uses the backup service's import check, which main.go hands it (CheckSource), so both refuse the same networks, allow-listed or not (TestSupabaseSourceRefusesThePlatformNetwork).

    Spec and code differ

    V1 §6.8 has the operator choose a tier for an import. ImportRequest has none: imports always create a shared project, to be promoted afterwards.

    Metadata self-backups and disaster recovery#

    runMetadataBackup has any agent dump XENIBASE_METADATA_BACKUP_URL (default XENIBASE_DATABASE_URL, off to disable) to metadata/ on the default target, in the Xenibase format, nightly at the window's start (V1 §11.6). A failure is a critical alert. docs/disaster-recovery.md rebuilds a lost control node from three things kept off it (the .env with the master key, the backup key file, the bucket credentials): start the metadata database, decrypt the newest metadata/ object with xenibase-agent decrypt, pg_restore --clean it, start everything (the pooler configuration is rendered again), re-register agents whose state was lost, and restore lost databases into new projects. Project-key backups also restore with gpg, pg_restore and wal-g alone.

    Note

    The metadata is as old as its last dump: projects, targets and project keys created since are gone from it, though their objects remain in the bucket. A project key exists only sealed in the metadata and in a download its admin may never have made, so such a key, or every project key once the master key is lost, leaves its .dump.gpg backups unreadable; the platform key file does not open them.

    Alerts#

    internal/alerts raises backup_failed (critical) when the latest backup, base backup or metadata backup failed, restore_test_failed (critical), wal_archive (critical) when a dedicated project's WAL archiving failed in the last 15 minutes or a completed segment has waited longer than that (WALArchiveSamples, from the collector's wal_archive_* metrics, which /metrics also serves), and backup_overdue (warning) for a project the scheduler backs up, older than 26 hours, with no backup in 26 hours (OverdueBackups). Any of them turns the public status page's Backups component to degraded (States).

    Resolved

    "Backup overdue" used to fire for projects the scheduler skips on purpose: OverdueBackups checked only status = 'active' and age, but the scheduler skips paused and archived projects (whose status stays active), branches without backups, and suspended or deleting organisations, so one sleeping Free project kept "Some backups are delayed or failing" on the public status page indefinitely. Now OverdueBackups applies ProjectsDueForBackup's filters: lifecycle = 'active', a branch only with branch_backups, an active organisation (TestBackupOverdueSkipsWhatTheSchedulerSkips). A project woken or reinstated after a day or more still fires until its next nightly backup, which is late in fact; without storage or the backup key the scheduler queues nothing, and every project fires.

    Failure handling#

    If this happensWhat Xenibase does
    No default target or backup keyNothing is scheduled; manual backups and restores answer 409; a delete logs "final backup skipped" and proceeds
    The worker or agent dies mid-dumpThe operation is reclaimed; the next attempt fails the old row and starts again; orphaned rows are failed hourly
    An upload outlives its attemptcleanFailed deletes failed rows' objects, 100 at a time, retrying unreachable targets later
    Retention cannot delete an objectA warning; the row stays and is tried after the next backup
    An object is truncated, altered, or under another keyThe restore or test fails on the first bad chunk, the missing final chunk, or the OpenPGP MDC, and is rolled back
    A restore into a new project failsOne retry on an empty database, then rollback
    An in-place restore failsThe safety backup goes back; if that fails, error with the route paused
    WAL cannot be flushed, or recovery does not finish409 before anything is created; or the new project is rolled back after ReadyTimeout
    A cross-region copy fails its checksumcopy_status = 'failed', retried after an hour
    A dedicated instance's WAL archiving fails or falls behindThe critical wal_archive alert within minutes, resolved once 15 minutes pass with no failed attempt and no segment waiting that long
    An import's URL is gone, or a table did not importThe import fails and the project is rolled back

    Branches are built from these restores (Database branches); who may take, restore and download backups is on Security and tenant isolation.

    Part C · Data safety

    Database branches

    Branches as shared-tier copies of a parent: from a backup or live, schema only, reset, detach and expiry.

    Checked against c67d14d · 2026-10-29
