    Xenibase runs more than one Postgres major at a time. Each major has a place in its life, kept in one table, and each instance runs an image built for its major. Minor releases are a restart on the same data, done by a background sweep in a weekly window. A major upgrade is a move: the project's database is copied by logical replication into a new instance (or a shared cluster) of the newer major, and the route is switched.

    • pgversions280 linesThe Postgres version lifecycle (V4.1 §6.1): an admin promotes a preview, deprecates a major with a retirement date at least 180 days ahead, or retires it; the owners and admins of every organisation with a project on a deprecated maj…

    Which majors are offered#

    Two things decide whether a major can be used. The server is configured with the majors it has images for, XENIBASE_PG_VERSIONS, default 17,18 (config). The pg_versions table says where each major is in its life (00046_pg_versions.sql). The first time the server looks, ensureVersions inserts every configured major as supported with ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING, so an operator's statuses are never overwritten. A major dropped from the setting keeps its row and is listed as not installed. Versions joins the two and counts the live projects on each.

    The image is a template. The agent's XENIBASE_AGENT_PG_IMAGE defaults to xenibase-postgres:{major}-walg3.0.9, and ImageFor replaces {major} with the instance spec's PGVersion (18 when it is 0). One Dockerfile builds every major: PG_MAJOR picks a stage built from the official postgres image of that major's pinned minor release (PG17_RELEASE, PG18_RELEASE), and WAL-G (a pinned commit), Patroni (a pinned version) and hypopg are added on top. Two checks keep an instance on the major it asked for:

    • After start, checkMajor runs postgres -V in the container and refuses a different major. An image name without {major} serves one version only, and this is where that shows.
    • PGDATA is set per major inside the instance's named volume, /var/lib/postgresql/{major}/docker (pgdataFor). The 17 image declares /var/lib/postgresql/data as an anonymous volume, and data there was lost on a recreate (decision M18 #9).

    The agent is built on postgres:18, so its pg_dump is 18. A newer major needs the agent image rebuilt before dumps of it work.

    The lifecycle#

    A major is preview, supported, deprecated or retired. The table's check constraint requires a retires_at on a deprecated row. No job ever flips a deprecated major to retired: EffectiveStatus reports a deprecated major as retired once retires_at has passed, everywhere the status is read (decision V4.1-M5 #3).

    StatusNew projectNew project, preview asked forUpgrade targetNew shared clusterRestore, branch or detached replica of a project on itDefault for new projects
    previewRefusedYesRefusedYesYesNever
    supportedYesYesYesYesYesThe newest installed one
    deprecatedYesYesRefusedYesYesOnly when no supported major is installed
    retiredRefusedRefusedRefusedYesYesNever

    The middle five columns are the five uses CheckVersion is called with: ForProject, ForPreviewProject, ForUpgrade, ForCluster and ForDerived. A major not in XENIBASE_PG_VERSIONS is refused for every use, whatever its row says.

    ForCluster allows a preview major, for the projects trying it, and a retired one on purpose: a cluster for the projects still on it. ForDerived returns before the status is looked at: the source's data is on that major already.

    Changing a status#

    A platform admin changes a major with PATCH /api/v1/admin/pg-versions/{major} (UpdatePgVersion, Admin → Platform → Postgres versions). One endpoint covers every transition, and pgversions.Change enforces the rules:

    • Preview only stays preview: no major goes back to it.
    • Supported from anything: promoting a preview, or taking a deprecation or retirement back.
    • Deprecated needs retires_at at least 180 days ahead (MinNotice). Deprecating again keeps deprecated_at and may move the date. Only a fresh deprecation sends the first notice.
    • Retired is refused while a live project runs on the major, unless its date has passed. Projects are never upgraded automatically: an upgrade can break an app.

    Notices to organisations#

    On a deprecation, and again 90, 30 and 7 days before retirement (Reminders), the owners and admins of every organisation with a project on the major get one email listing those projects, each with a link to its Upgrade card. Sweep runs hourly (pgVersionSvc.Run(bgCtx, time.Hour) in cmd/server) and sends only the nearest step reached, so a server that was down past a step sends one mail, not several; before the first reminder it sends the deprecation notice to any organisation that has not had it. notifyOrg inserts a pg_version_notices row keyed on major, organisation and step in a transaction that stays open until the mail is sent, and skips the organisation when the insert finds a row already there. A second server's insert waits on the first's and then finds the row, so the sweep is safe to run on two servers at once, and a send that fails rolls the row back, so the next sweep tries again. Projects on a deprecated or retired major show a banner (VersionBanner), red once it is retired: "keeps running but is unsupported".

    Resolved

    A notice whose email failed used never to be resent: notify committed the pg_version_notices row before sending, so a mail server that was down for the deprecation or a reminder meant that organisation never heard of it. Now the row is committed only with a successful send (notifyOrg), still under the insert's row lock, so two servers still send once, and the sweep also retries the deprecation notice until the first reminder is due (TestNoticeIsResentAfterAFailedSend).

    How new projects pick a major#

    provision.Create resolves the requested major with CheckVersion, as ForPreviewProject when the create form's preview box was ticked. A request without a major gets DefaultVersion: the newest installed supported major, else the newest installed deprecated one, else an error. A shared project then needs a running shared cluster of that major in its region (PickSharedInstance filters on pg_version), and otherwise fails with no_capacity. A dedicated project gets an instance of that major. Preview and retired majors are refused with a message saying what to choose instead. A deprecated major is still open: decision V4.1-M5 #2 keeps it so, to avoid surprising owners in the middle of a migration.

    Every other way of making a project goes through the same Create with the source's major and Derived set, checked as ForDerived: a branch (branching.Create), a point-in-time recovery (backup.PITR) and a detached read replica. A project on a retired or preview major can do all three. Moves, promotions and demotions do not create a project and do not check the status.

    Resolved

    A project on a retired or preview major used to be unable to recover to a point in time, branch, or detach a replica: all three called provision.Create with the source's major as ForProject, which refuses retired and preview majors, so the owner of a retired-major project who dropped a table could not get it back from the WAL archive, and every preview project was in the same position from the day it was made. Now the three set CreateParams.Derived, and CheckVersion takes ForDerived: any major in XENIBASE_PG_VERSIONS, whatever its status. The comment on ForCluster now says what it allows. TestCheckVersionForDerived and TestCreateDerivedOnARetiredMajor cover it.

    Minor releases#

    A minor release (18.1 to 18.2) changes binaries only, so an upgrade is a restart of the same volume on a newer image. The operator rebuilds or pulls the image tags on each node (make pg-image, install.sh, or docker pull; docs/upgrade.md). Nothing in Xenibase pulls a newer image: the agent pulls a tag only when it is missing.

    1. Releases are read. Every five minutes MaintenanceSweep first calls CheckReleases for running instances not checked in the last hour. The agent's info reads PG_VERSION from two images: the one the container was created from (pg_release, only while it runs) and the one its tag names now (pg_release_available). An instance whose container is not running is left as it was recorded. Clusters the server was configured with, which have no agent, are skipped.
    2. Inside the window (DefaultWindow: Sunday 02:00 to 06:00 UTC, one platform-wide setting), InstancesBehind lists instances whose two releases differ, dedicated before shared, leaving out any whose last upgrade to that release failed. NewerRelease keeps those where the tag is a later minor of the same major.
    3. One instance per sweep. An instance with a project that is not active or has an operation queued or running is skipped (InstanceBusy). An HA instance waits for maintenance announced to its project at least 72 hours before (announced), unless XENIBASE_MAINTENANCE_REQUIRE_ANNOUNCEMENT=false. proposeMaintenance drafts that announcement for the first window at least the draft lead away. The first instance that passes gets a minor_upgrade operation (EnqueueMinorUpgrade), exclusive with its projects' other operations, and the sweep returns; nothing more is queued while it is queued or running. One server sweeps at a time, under an advisory lock (LockedMaintenanceSweep).
    4. The restart (minorUpgrade, run by the operation). The minor_upgrades row is recorded when it is queued; it freezes every project database on the instance at the poolers (Freeze: PAUSE on the transaction pooler, falling back to KILL after 10 seconds; KILL on the session pooler). It calls Recreate and then RESUME. Read replicas of an instance without HA follow one at a time, each out of rotation meanwhile (recreateReplicas).
    5. HA instances are switched over, not restarted (minorUpgradeHA): each standby and read replica is recreated and waited for, the leader is switched over to a standby, and the old leader is recreated as a standby. Writes pause only for the switchover.

    On the agent, a recreate stops the container (60 seconds, then a kill), renames it aside (xenibase-<id>-previous), and creates a new one from the tag on the same volume. The old one is removed only once the new one is ready; otherwise putBack removes the new one and starts the old one again:

    A shared cluster is upgraded the same way, after every dedicated instance, with all its projects frozen together. The bundle's own cluster from compose.yaml has no agent and is left to the operator. An admin can also upgrade one instance at once, outside the window and past the announcement gate (MinorUpgradeNow, POST /api/v1/admin/instances/{instance_id}/minor-upgrade).

    Resolved

    A failed minor upgrade used to leave the instance down, and the sweep then forgot it. The agent removed the old container before creating the new one, so a new release that could not be created, started or made ready left nothing running under a row that still said running; the sweep retried the same instance every 5 minutes, freezing its projects each time, with no other instance upgraded meanwhile; and once CheckReleases ran again a missing container reported no release and a crash-looping one the new release, so the outage looked like a finished upgrade. Now the agent keeps the old container, stopped and renamed, until the new one is ready and puts it back otherwise, even when the server's request was cancelled; a create that finds only the set-aside container (an agent stopped part-way) renames it back. info reports a release only for a running container, and CheckReleases records nothing for one that is not. On the server, Recreate records the restored container's address, or says the instance is down; the failure is kept in minor_upgrades, InstancesBehind leaves out an instance whose last upgrade to its image's release failed, so the sweep moves on to the next one, and a minor_upgrade_failed alert fires until an upgrade of it succeeds. A newer release or Upgrade now tries it again. The instance is not marked error: the old container normally runs again, and an empty shared cluster in error would be reaped. TestRecreatePutsTheOldContainerBack, TestCreatePutsBackAContainerARecreateLeft, TestInfoReportsNoReleaseWhenStopped, TestInstancesBehindSkipsAFailedUpgrade and TestMinorUpgradeFailedCondition cover it.

    Resolved

    The minor-upgrade sweep used to take no lock and keep no state that survived a crash. Two servers picked the same first instance and restarted it twice, the first one's RESUME letting clients in while the second had it down, and a server that stopped between Freeze and Resume left PgBouncer paused with nothing to resume it. Now the sweep holds a session advisory lock on a connection of its own, and each upgrade is a minor_upgrade operation, exclusive with the projects' other operations: a crash hands it to another worker, whose attempt resumes the poolers first, and its OnFail (failMinorUpgrade) resumes them and finishes the run. A minor_upgrades row left unfinished with no operation to finish it (a run from before this change, or an OnFail cut short) is finished by the next sweep after resuming its instance's poolers. Upgrade now (MinorUpgradeNow) queues the same operation and waits for it. See Dedicated instances, HA and moves for the tests.

    Resolved

    The image tag used not to pin the Postgres release: FROM ${REGISTRY}postgres:${PG_MAJOR} took whatever minor the official tag held when a node built or pulled it, so xenibase-postgres:18-walg3.0.9 named different releases on different nodes, any recreate outside the window landed on whatever the tag held there, and the previous release, no longer tagged, could not be pointed back at after a regression. Now the Dockerfile builds each major from a pinned release (ARG PG17_RELEASE=17.11, PG18_RELEASE=18.6, overridable), and build.sh, which make pg-image and install.sh run, tags it both xenibase-postgres:18-walg3.0.9 (the agent's {major} template, unchanged, so upgrades keep working) and with the release it holds, xenibase-postgres:18.6-walg3.0.9, so the release a rebuild replaces stays on the node and the major tag can be pointed back at it. The server still does not choose a release per instance: every instance of a major on a node runs what its major tag names. TestInstanceImagePinsTheRelease checks the Dockerfile and the script.

    Spec and code differ

    V3 §2.4 asks for "a weekly maintenance window per region". There is one window for the platform, stored under the maintenance_window setting and read in UTC. Decision M18 #11 deferred per-region windows to M25 (regions), and they have not arrived.

    Major upgrades of dedicated projects#

    A major upgrade is not pg_upgrade. It is a move (decision M18 #10): a new instance of the target major, of the same size, on the project's own node, filled by logical replication while the old one keeps serving, then a cutover of a few seconds. pg_upgrade would need both majors' binaries in one container and a longer outage. Members with the ProjectPromote permission run it from the project's settings (POST /api/v1/projects/{id}/upgrade/preflight, then …/upgrade), and the deprecation emails link there.

    The preflight#

    UpgradePreflight changes nothing and returns a list of checks, each ok, warning or blocked:

    CheckBlocks when
    targetHA is on, or the project has read replicas (both must be removed first and set up again after), or a shared project has no shared cluster of the target major in its region open to its organisation, or a dedicated project's node is not active or has no room for a second instance of its size.
    versionThe target is not supported (ForUpgrade), or is not newer than the current major.
    extensionsThe target cannot create an extension the project uses (logical.Preflight).
    replicationNever. A warning when logical replication is not possible (large objects, unlogged tables, no free slot or WAL sender): the copy is then a pg_dump piped into pg_restore during the freeze, and writes pause for its whole length, estimated at 40 MB/s plus 5 seconds.
    deprecatedNever. A warning for each name the new major removed that appears in a function body, view or per-database setting (Removals, matched by whole word).
    schemaThe schema does not restore on the target major.

    The schema check is a real restore. For a dedicated project, scratchTrial starts a temporary instance of the target major on the project's node: 0.5 CPU, 512 MB, profile scratch, no WAL-G. schemaTrial then creates a short-lived non-superuser login and database there, creates the project's extensions as the superuser, and restores a schema-only, owner-less dump as that login with errors allowed. Each error becomes a blocked line. The temporary instance is destroyed and marked deleted when the check ends, success or not, and if that destroy fails the orphan reaper removes it once it is an hour old (it leaves a younger one alone, since the check may still be using it). A shared project's check runs the same restore in a scratch database on the target cluster. Upgrade runs the whole preflight again and refuses if anything is blocked.

    The upgrade#

    1. Queued. In the transaction that sets the project to upgrading and queues a major_upgrade operation (EnqueueExclusiveTx), Upgrade inserts the target instance row: same node, the source's CPU, memory, volume and pitr_days, max_connections at least the source's, its own WAL-G prefix. It refuses if the project moved since the check, or if the node no longer has room for a second instance of that size.
    2. The target starts. The operation runs runMove, the node move's handler (Kinds: two attempts, 48 hours), which calls Ensure for the new instance.
    3. Roles are restored before any data (prepareTarget): the database and owner with the same SCRAM verifier (Prepare), member logins and the read-only role (SyncMemberRoles), integrator roles with the owner's admin option (restoreIntegratorRoles), the roles the owner created with role management, with attributes, password and memberships (restoreOwnedRoles), and NOLOGIN stand-ins for any other role that a grant, policy or owner in the database names (placeholderRoles). So existing passwords keep working on the new major.
    4. The copy (copyForMove). The schema goes first (copyKeepingOwners). Then a publication FOR ALL TABLES and a subscription copy the rows, not in binary mode, since the majors differ. Schema changes are paused on the project until the move finishes. The source keeps serving reads and writes.
    5. The freeze and cutover. When the subscription has caught up, freeze makes the owner and member logins NOLOGIN, pauses the poolers and ends remaining sessions. logical.Cutover waits up to 30 seconds for the last commits, copies sequences with a margin of 1,000 and compares sampled tables. One transaction then points the project at the new instance and records the old one in retired_databases for 48 hours (RetainSource). The old base backups get an expiry instead of being deleted.
    6. Finishing (finishMove, idempotent). It syncs and resumes the poolers, sets the project active, removes the replication objects (a slot left behind would keep WAL forever), stops the old instance (retireSource), and takes the first base backup on the new one. Clients reconnect to the same URL.

    Downtime is the freeze: the decisions record 115 ms for a 1 GB move and 135 ms for 3 GB under continuous writes (M18 #12). In dump mode it is the whole copy. Rollback covers only the time before the cutover: failMove removes the replication objects, makes the source's logins LOGIN again, resumes the poolers, sets the project active and destroys the new instance. A source that cannot be reached still gets its poolers resumed, and the project stays upgrading until RepairStuckMoves gives its logins back. After the cutover the only failure handling is to run the finishing steps again.

    Resolved

    The orphan reaper used to destroy an upgrade's target after five minutes. ListOrphanedInstances took any dedicated instance older than 5 minutes that no live project pointed at for a failed create's leftover, and a major upgrade's target is inserted when the operation is queued but pointed at only at the cutover. So any upgrade whose queue wait, schema copy and initial sync took more than five minutes lost its target and its WAL-G prefix part-way and rolled back, and a pass that listed the target just before a cutover would have destroyed the live instance. Node moves, promotions and resizes that move had the same problem. Now the query skips an instance a queued or running operation names as its target_instance and a scratch instance in its first hour, and ReapOrphans checks each instance again just before destroying it (TestListOrphanedInstancesSkipsAnOperationsTarget).

    Resolved

    Recovering to a time before a major upgrade used to fail. PITRWindow and BaseBackupBefore offer the old instance's base backups, since they select by project, but backup.PITR created the new project with the current instance's major, so a 17 base backup was started in a Postgres 18 container, which refuses the data ("database files are incompatible with server"). Now PlanPITR names the instance that took the base backup as the source (backupInstance: archives live under instances/<id>/, so the backup's prefix names it, running or kept stopped), which also gives the restore that instance's superuser, the one in its data; and PITR takes the major from it (SourceMajor), checked as ForDerived so its status does not matter. An owner whose app breaks on the new major restores to before the upgrade on the old one (TestPITRStartsTheBaseBackupsMajor).

    Risk

    Nothing points a project back at its retained instance. The old instance is kept stopped for 48 hours, but no API, UI or command starts it again as the project's. Doing that without losing data needs the writes made since the cutover copied back, and the move machinery cannot: it copies into an empty target from scratch, and nothing records a replication position on the new instance that matches the old one at the cutover. Re-pointing it as it is would silently drop every write since the upgrade, which is what a point-in-time recovery to before the upgrade already gives, under a new project, without touching the live one. A safe re-point needs a reverse logical slot created at the cutover (or a full reverse move into the retained instance) and is left for later.

    Resolved

    The upgrade's target used to skip the capacity check and drop the PITR add-on. A node move builds its target through Validate, which checks that the size fits the node, and copies pitr_days; Upgrade did neither, so on a full node a second instance of the same size was created anyway on the node's one disk beside the source, and a project paying for 14 or 30 days of point-in-time recovery silently got 7, and was billed for 7. Now upgradeRoom runs the same fits check for the source's size on its node (and refuses a draining node): the preflight's target check is blocked when it fails, and insertUpgradeTarget checks again in the queueing transaction and refuses with the reason, telling the owner to move the project to a node with room first. The target takes the source's pitr_days, and a resized source's size is named custom rather than small (TestUpgradeTargetChecksRoomAndKeepsPITRDays).

    Shared projects on an old major#

    A shared project lives on a cluster of its major, and nothing moves it off when the major is deprecated or retired. It keeps running there, and new shared clusters of a retired major may still be added for it. Its upgrade uses the same preflight and handler: the target is the least-loaded shared cluster of the newer major in its region that its organisation may use, the schema is tried in a scratch database there, and the move copies into that cluster (no new instance, so a rollback drops the partial copy instead). The old database is kept read-only (default_transaction_read_only) for 48 hours. A shared project needs such a cluster first: "no shared cluster runs Postgres 18 yet (Admin → Nodes → Add shared cluster)". V3 §2.4 asks for "one shared cluster per supported version in each region", and nothing creates one automatically.

    See Backups, restores and imports for what is archived before and after an upgrade, Dedicated instances, HA and moves for switchovers, and Connections: poolers and the edge for how the poolers hold clients during a freeze.

    Failure handling#

    What failsWhat happens
    A notice emailLogged, and its pg_version_notices row rolled back: the hourly sweep sends it again until it goes, or until a later step supersedes it. A deprecation withdrawn and made again sends no new first notice to organisations that had one, since their rows remain.
    A retirement date passesNothing runs. Every read sees the major as retired from that moment.
    A project on the instance is busyThe instance waits for a later sweep.
    An HA instance has no announcementIt waits. A draft announcement is proposed for the first window far enough away.
    Pausing the poolers failsEverything paused so far is resumed, the run is recorded as failed, and the instance is not touched.
    The server stops during an upgradeThe operation's lease runs out and another worker runs it once more, resuming the poolers first; a last attempt that fails runs OnFail, which resumes them and records the failure.
    The recreate failsThe agent starts the old container again. Recorded in minor_upgrades with the error, which says if even the old container would not start; an alert fires, and the sweep skips the instance until a newer release or Upgrade now.
    An HA upgrade stops after the switchoverThe new leader runs the new release, so the instance no longer looks behind. The old leader stays a standby on the old release until something recreates it.
    A major upgrade fails before the cutoverRetried once from a clean target database. Then failMove: the source serves again with no data lost, and the new instance is destroyed.
    A major upgrade fails after the cutoverThe retry and OnFail both run only the finishing steps (route, resume, cleanup, stop the old instance, first backup).
    The worker dies part-wayThe operation's lease runs out and another worker takes it up. See the operations queue.

    Part D · Backend services

    The data API

    Backend services' control side and the data API on the edge: the xb_* schemas, roles and keys, the catalog, reads, writes and RPC, the schema editor and generated types.

    Backend services (V4) give a project an HTTP API at https://<ref>.<domain>: the data API, auth, storage and realtime. This page covers the data API and what it stands on. On the control plane, internal/services turns services on, makes the roles, schemas and keys, and feeds the edge. On the edge, data.go, datasql.go, datawrite.go and rpc.go turn each request into one parameterised statement. How the edge finds a project, checks keys and tokens and opens the transaction is on Connections, and is not repeated here.

    • services8,466 linesBackend services' control-plane side (V4 §2): enabling and disabling them per project (roles and xb_* schemas in the project database, API keys, the signing key), keeping the roles current when a project moves, and the configuration fe…
    • datacat451 linesReads the parts of a project database the data API serves (V4 §3): relations, columns, keys, foreign keys and functions in the exposed schemas. xenibase-edge caches it per project; xenibase-server uses it for type generation and the security…
    • schemaedit1,023 linesTurns a schema-change request from the visual editor into DDL, risk notes, and a reverse migration (V2 §4.3).
    • typegen667 linesWrites typed definitions of a project's tables, views and functions for the SDKs (V4 §3.7): TypeScript, Dart and Go, from the data API's catalog.

    Turning services on#

    POST /api/v1/projects/{id}/services needs project.services, the project admin role and the admin token scope (ServicesManage). Enable locks the project row, requires it active with no operation in flight, makes the project_services row with a new 8-character ref (NewRef: a letter, then seven of an alphabet without 0, o, 1 and l), and queues enable_services. If the project has no live key, the same transaction makes a publishable and a secret key and returns them once.

    The operation, enableOn, runs four steps. Each can be repeated, so the three attempts the operation gets are safe:

    1. Roles. ensureRolesOn creates or repairs five roles on the instance, as the platform's admin.
    2. Schemas. applySchema brings xb_auth, xb_storage and xb_realtime to the newest version, each version in one transaction.
    3. Signing key. ensureJWTKey makes an ES256 key unless one is active. The private half is sealed with the master keyring, with the row's id as associated data (jwtAAD), so a sealed key copied to another row does not open.
    4. On. SetServicesEnabled, then SyncPooler so the poolers know the new logins. The feed then carries the project to the edges.

    The roles#

    Names come from store/names.go. Every role is NOSUPERUSER NOCREATEDB NOCREATEROLE NOREPLICATION NOINHERIT with a connection limit:

    RoleUsed forAttributes
    <db>_anonPublishable key, no user tokenNOBYPASSRLS, limit 20
    <db>_userPublishable key and a user's access tokenNOBYPASSRLS, limit 20
    <db>_serviceSecret keyBYPASSRLS, limit 20
    <db>_auth_hookPostgres auth hooks (Project auth)NOBYPASSRLS, limit 10
    <db>_edgeThe edge's own login: the xb_auth tables, storage bookkeeping, realtime's outboxNOBYPASSRLS, limit 20, no memberships

    Each password is derived from the master key and the role's name (edgePassword) and never stored; project_services keeps the SCRAM verifiers for the poolers. The edge connects as the request's role itself. Before M32 the edge login could SET ROLE to the request roles, so a RESET ROLE in tenant code reached it; ensureRolesOn revokes any such membership it still finds (V4-M32 #18). On the shared tier the request roles also get the shared temp_file_limit.

    The xb_* schemas and the grants#

    schemaVersions is an ordered list of statement lists. The {{anon}}-style placeholders are filled in with quoted role names by expand. The schemas belong to the platform's admin, and PUBLIC has nothing on them.

    VersionAdds
    1The three schemas. xb_auth.claims(), claim(name), role() and uid(), which read current_setting('xb.claims'). The request roles' grants on public.
    2Auth's tables (users, identities, sessions, refresh tokens, one-time codes, audit log). Only the edge login may use them. The user_profiles view lets a user see their own row, and the service role and the owner see every row.
    3OAuth flow state, MFA factors and challenges, aal(), is_anonymous(), and the hook role's grants.
    4Storage: buckets, objects (with row-level security, owned by the project's owner so the owner can write the policies), uploads, garbage and usage (Storage).
    5Realtime: captured tables, the outbox, enable/disable, channel access and history (Realtime).
    6xb_auth.idempotency with idempotency_claim and idempotency_store, for the user and service roles only (writes).
    7Takes back the request roles' EXECUTE on extensions' functions. xb_auth.withheld, grant_targets and sync_grants, which only the edge login and the platform may run.

    Version 1 grants table privileges to every role on every table in public, and the default privileges do the same for the owner's later tables. That is a deliberate choice (docs/decisions.md, V4-M28 #8): which rows a caller reaches is left to row-level security, with the edge's RLS gate in front. For anon and user, grantTablesStmt grants a relation only where the role holds nothing on it yet, so running version 1 again after a move or restore puts lost grants back without undoing the owner's own REVOKEs. Then xb_auth.sync_grants (version 7) takes back from anon and user every privilege on a relation that does not protect itself: a table or foreign table without row-level security, a materialized view, a view that runs as its owner. They keep SELECT on a public table. It records what it took in xb_auth.withheld and gives exactly that back once the table has row-level security (or, for SELECT, is listed public). The control plane runs it after every schema run and when the public tables change. The edge runs it as its own login, in a transaction of its own, whenever a project's catalog fingerprint changes (the catalog). So the usual order, a table, then row-level security and policies, works as before, and a table that loses row-level security loses its grants within the catalog's 2 seconds. Extensions' tables and the xb_* schemas are left alone. A schema exposed later gets the same statements, exposureStmts, run by applyExposure. Removing a schema from the list revokes nothing. The data API stops serving that schema, but the grants stay, so functions and views in a schema that is still exposed can go on reading it.

    Resolved

    The grants used to reach extension functions locked away from PUBLIC, and the API served them. GRANT EXECUTE ON ALL FUNCTIONS IN SCHEMA public ran as the platform's admin, so it also covered what an extension installed there, and pg_stat_statements (on the shared tier's list, SharedExtensions) revokes pg_stat_statements_reset from PUBLIC because the statistics belong to the whole instance. <db>_anon held EXECUTE on it, datacat listed it, and POST /data/v1/rpc/pg_stat_statements_reset with the publishable key emptied every tenant's Query Insights on a shared cluster. Now version 1 and the exposure grants grant each function on its own (grantFunctionsStmt) and leave out any with an extension dependency (pg_depend, deptype e); the owner's later functions still get EXECUTE from the default privileges. Version 7 revokes EXECUTE on extensions' functions from the three request roles, so a project enabled before reaches the same state on its next reconcile. datacat leaves extensions' functions out, so the API answers 404 unknown_function for them and type generation and the advisor no longer list them. TestExtensionFunctionsStayLocked installs the extension, applies the versions, puts the old grant back and runs version 7, and calls the function through the edge.

    API keys#

    GenerateKey makes xb_pub_ plus 32 characters or xb_sec_ plus 40, drawn with crypto/rand from 57 symbols (about 187 and 233 bits). Only the hex SHA-256 is stored (edgeapi.HashKey), with a prefix of the first six characters for lists. A publishable key is also kept in display, because it is meant to be shown. A secret key appears once, in the response that made it. A key this random needs no salt or slow hash. CreateKey adds a named key for rotation, and RevokeKey reaches the edges with the next feed change, which carries only live keys' hashes.

    Turning services off#

    Disable sets enabled false and revokes every key in one transaction, so the edge stops at its next feed read. The queued disable_services takes the logins off the poolers, sets every role NOLOGIN and ends their sessions. The xb_* schemas and their data stay (V4 §2.4). Enabling again makes new keys and logs the roles back in.

    Moves, restores and branches#

    Roles belong to an instance, but schemas and grants belong to the database. Three paths keep them together:

    • Promotion, demotion and moves copy grants to the target, and the grants fail if the roles are missing. The dedicated service first calls EnsureRolesOn (ServiceRoles in cmd/server), which creates the roles there without recording anything.
    • The reconciler. Reconcile runs every 15 seconds on ServicesToReconcile: enabled, active projects whose roles_instance is not their instance or whose schema version is behind. For a moved project it repairs the roles, takes the xb_* objects back from whoever restored them (reownSQL), and runs every version again, then the exposure grants.
    • A database made again (an in-place restore, a branch reset) calls MarkForReconcile through provision.DatabaseRecreated. It clears roles_instance, so the next pass does all of the above.

    The ref, keys and signing key survive all of these, so URLs and apps' keys keep working. A branch instead gets an API of its own: a new ref, keys and signing key, without the parent's sessions (Database branches).

    The catalog#

    datacat.Introspect reads what the API serves from the system catalogs. It reads relations in the exposed schemas (tables, partitioned tables, views, materialized views and foreign tables, but not partitions, at most 5,000), their columns with type, category, nullability, defaults, generated and enum labels, primary and foreign keys between exposed relations, and functions (prokind = 'f', not trigger functions or an extension's) with their arguments, defaults, volatility, SECURITY DEFINER and result columns. The edge, type generation, the API page (Describe) and the advisor all read it, so they describe the same API (V4-M30 #6).

    • Exposed schemas: public by default, 1 to 10, matching ^[a-z_][a-z0-9_]{0,62}$, never pg_*, xb_*, information_schema or xenibase (validExposure). applyExposure refuses a schema that does not exist. A name resolves as schema.table, or as a bare name in the first exposed schema that has it (Catalog.Find).
    • Public tables: up to 200 names (table in public, or schema.table) that anon and user may read without row-level security. They may never be written without it.

    The edge keeps one catalog per project, shared by every role, because pg_catalog reads the same for all of them (catalog). A request uses the cached copy if it was checked less than 2 seconds ago. Otherwise it runs FingerprintSQL in the request's transaction. That query sums xmin and counts rows of pg_constraint and pg_proc in the exposed schemas, and of pg_class, pg_attribute and pg_policy in every schema of the project's, because privileges, row-level security and policies on a table outside the exposed schemas matter to the views and functions inside them, and to the cache. A changed result means the edge runs sync_grants (the grants), reads the catalog again, and records each request role's Reach for the gate. A 42P01 or 42703 from Postgres also drops it (pgAPIError). The catalog survives feed updates (apply carries it over).

    Reads#

    data routes /data/v1/… by method and segment count. It decodes each segment on its own, so an escaped / stays inside its name.

    RequestDoes
    GET /data/v1/{table}A list: select, where (repeatable), or, order, limit, offset, cursor, count. Any other parameter is 400 unknown_parameter.
    GET /data/v1/{table}/{pk}One row by a single-column primary key, or 404.
    POST /data/v1/{table}/queryThe same as JSON (at most 1 MB), with nested and/or/not, 8 levels deep, and JSON values (filterFromJSON).
    GET /data/v1/openapi.jsonThe project's OpenAPI document, for the secret key only (openAPI).
    POST|PATCH|DELETE /data/v1/{table}[/{pk}], /batch, /rpc/{fn}Writes and functions.

    The rule (V4-M29 #2) is that names come only from the catalog and are quoted, and values only ever travel as parameters cast to the column's type. Request names must match identRe (no whitespace, quotes, backslashes, commas, parentheses, :, ! or >), but the SQL is built from the catalog's own *Column and *Table: builder.column looks each name up and qi quotes the catalog's spelling. Only JSON path keys reach the text from the request, through lit. Casts use format_type output from the catalog. FuzzReadSQL fuzzes the builder.

    • Select (ParseSelect): columns, alias:column, *, JSON paths (meta->plan, only on json and jsonb), and relations name(…) or name!hint(…) to 3 levels, 200 items per level. A row is row_to_json of a subselect.
    • Embedding (resolveEmbed) goes through a foreign key. The name can be the related table's name, or the column without _id. If two foreign keys fit, the request gets 400 ambiguous_relation rather than a guess. To-one becomes LIMIT 1 of a correlated subquery. To-many becomes json_agg of at most 1,000 rows, ordered by the target's key. Every embedded relation goes through the gate too.
    • Filters (where): eq neq lt lte gt gte compare as the column's type, in as = ANY($n::text[]::type[]), like and ilike on ::text, is null, true or false, contains and contained_by as @> and <@, and search with websearch_to_tsquery. A request may use at most 30 conditions. A JSON path compares as text.
    • Order and pages. orderKeys adds the primary key to the requested order, so pages are stable. A cursor is base64 JSON of the last row's key values as text plus a hash of the table and order (orderSig), so it cannot be replayed on another order. after builds the keyset condition with Postgres's default null placement. limit is 1 to 1,000 (default 100), and offset at most 10,000, not combined with a cursor.
    • Counts. exact runs count(*) under a savepoint with a 2-second timeout and answers null if that runs out (countExact). estimated is the planner's row estimate.

    Postgres errors map to stable codes (pgErrors): 42501 becomes 403 permission_denied, a 22… becomes 400 invalid_value, 23505 becomes 409 unique_violation, 57014 becomes 504 statement_timeout, and so on. Unmapped errors become 400 database_error, or 503 for connection and resource classes.

    The RLS gate#

    The edge refuses anon and user what row-level security cannot protect (V4 §3.6). It checks the relation the URL names, every relation embedded, what a view reads, and, for a function, what the caller's role can reach:

    • Views. datacat follows each security_invoker view's rule through pg_rewrite and pg_depend, and through the invoker views it reads, and records the relations nothing protects (Unprotected) and whether it calls one of the project's functions (CallsFunctions). viewGate refuses a view that reads such a relation, unless it is a public table and the request is a read, and a view that calls a function when functionGate would refuse it.
    • Functions. A SECURITY INVOKER function reaches whatever the caller's role may, and no catalog can say what a PL/pgSQL body reads. On each catalog refresh the edge records, per role, the relations it holds privileges on that nothing protects (ReachSQL, Catalog.Reach; SELECT on a public table does not count). functionGate refuses every such function to that role while the list is not empty, with 403 rls_required naming the first. sync_grants normally keeps the list empty, so this is the backstop for a project behind version 7 or a grant the owner made by hand. A SECURITY DEFINER function runs as its owner and passes (the advisor flags it).

    writeGate is the same without the public-table exception, and a materialized view is never writable. The service role passes both. Column privileges are left to Postgres, and hiding a column takes the table-level SELECT away and grants the others. select=* expands to every column the catalog has, so a caller missing the privilege on one column gets 403 permission_denied for * and must name the columns it may read.

    Resolved

    The gate used to look only at the relation the URL named, while the grants reached every table. A table without row-level security answered 403 rls_required, and the advisor said "the publishable key can't reach this table", yet <db>_anon held SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE on it, so a security_invoker view over it, or any SECURITY INVOKER function reading it (rpc applied no gate), published it to anyone with the publishable key. Now three things stand in the way. Postgres itself refuses: sync_grants takes anon's and user's privileges on such a table back as soon as an edge sees it, and gives them back once the table has row-level security, so existing projects' tables with policies, and the invoker views and functions over them, keep working, and an owner's own column grants survive. The view gate checks what a view reads, through pg_depend. The function gate refuses invoker functions to a role that still reaches an unprotected relation. The advisor's rls_disabled message now says that the table is out of reach directly and through views and functions, and view_reads_unprotected names an invoker view over such a table. TestRLSGateReachesViewsAndFunctions runs the payments example through the edge, with a public table, a table that gains and loses row-level security, and a database without sync_grants.

    Resolved

    The documented way to hide a column used to do nothing. docs/backend-services.md and the advisor's secret_column fix said REVOKE SELECT (email) ON profiles FROM "<db>_anon", which Postgres ignores while anon holds table-level SELECT, as it did from version 1; and a full re-run of version 1 after a move would have put the table-level grant back anyway. Now the guide gives REVOKE SELECT ON profiles FROM … followed by GRANT SELECT (id, name, …), and the advisor's fix (hideColumnFix) does the same with the table's other columns, or gives the column REVOKE when anon holds only column grants. grantTablesStmt skips a relation the role holds column privileges on, and sync_grants leaves a table with row-level security alone, so the hiding survives both. TestHiddenColumnStaysHidden shows the old statement leaving the column readable, runs the advisor's fix, reads through the edge, and runs every version and the sync again.

    How a request runs#

    Every data API request is one call to WithRequest: one transaction through the transaction pooler, as the role's own login, with set_config('xb.claims', …, true) and set_config('statement_timeout', …, true) (Connections). For anon the claims are {"role":"anon"}, for the secret key {"role":"service"}, and for a user the verified token's claims. Policies read them through xb_auth.uid() and its siblings. Row-level security is Postgres's own, because the statement runs as <db>_anon or <db>_user, which are NOBYPASSRLS. GETs may go to read replicas (replicaRead).

    LimitValueWhere
    Statement timeout8 s by default, up to 15 s, within the plan's ceilingSettings.Validate, EffectiveSettings
    Rate600 a minute per IP, 12,000 per key, reduced under a spend capauthorize
    Rows, offset1 to 1,000 (100 by default), offset up to 10,000builder.read
    Filters, select, embeds30 conditions, 200 items, 3 levels, 1,000 embedded rowsdatasql.go constants
    Result10 MB, then 413 result_too_largeread, runWrite, rpc
    Body1 MB for a query, 8 MB for a writedata, readBody
    Estimated costmax_query_cost, 1,000,000 by default; 0 means the default, so it cannot be turned off. Reads, exact counts and set-returning functionscost, the feed (or(st.MaxQueryCost, DefaultMaxQueryCost))

    The cost guard runs EXPLAIN on every read's statement before running it, as the caller and with the request's own values, and refuses it with 400 query_too_expensive above the limit. Nothing is cached: planning a typical 100-row read took about 57 µs against about 265 µs to run it in a local measurement, so a plan per request is cheap next to the round trip. An exact count is planned too, and over the limit it is not run and answers count: null, as when it times out. A set-returning function's call is planned with its select, filters and limit, which sees through a SQL function the planner inlines (a PL/pgSQL body is a fixed estimate to the planner). Writes and scalar functions are bounded by the statement timeout alone.

    Resolved

    The first values to arrive used to set the cost for all later ones. cost kept one estimate per SQL text, and filter values are parameters, so where=kind:eq:click&limit=1000 (a short walk of the key) admitted where=kind:eq:nothing (a scan of the whole table) at the first request's cost, about 100 times too low; the cache was shared between roles, so a plan made for the service role, without policy predicates, admitted anon too. Exact counts and set-returning functions were not checked at all. Now every request is planned with its own values as its own role, exact counts and set-returning function calls go through the guard, and the per-shape cache is gone. TestCostGuardPlansEachRequest sends the cheap value and then the expensive one as the service role and as anon, an exact count over the limit and under it, and an inlined SQL function called with both values.

    The anonymous-read cache#

    A project can list tables (schema.table) and functions (rpc.name, rpc.schema.name) with a TTL of 1 to 3,600 seconds, at most 100 entries (cache_ttl_seconds, V4.1 §10). The edge then answers some GETs from an in-process LRU of 64 MB (respCache). A request is served from it only under all of these conditions:

    Anon's claims are a constant, so one anonymous caller's answer is every anonymous caller's answer, and no user's rows can get in. The key (cacheKey) is the ref, the feed version, the catalog's fingerprint, the path and the sorted query without apikey. A lookup happens before any transaction (read, rpc), against the fingerprint the edge last read, and only while that was checked less than 2 seconds ago (fingerprint); otherwise the request goes to the database, whose catalog check runs. The fingerprint covers pg_policy, privileges and row-level security, and when it changes the edge drops all of the project's entries. A committed write drops the entries that read the written table, through the main table or an embed, and every function result. A function called with POST drops all of the project's entries (dropTables). Each drop increments a per-project generation, and a read that began before the drop does not store its rows. Realtime's hub drops the tables it sees change on that edge. Anything else, such as SQL, jobs or another edge, shows within the TTL. Stored answers carry Cache-Control: public with Vary: Authorization, Read-Replica.

    Resolved

    Taking access away used to miss the cache. The fingerprint did not cover pg_policy, and a hit never opened a transaction, so after a DROP POLICY, an ALTER POLICY or a REVOKE a popular URL kept serving the rows for the rest of its TTL, up to an hour. Now FingerprintSQL sums pg_policy too, with pg_class (privileges, row-level security) across the project's schemas; a hit is served only while the catalog was checked within its 2 seconds, so a steady stream of hits still reaches the database once per interval; and a changed fingerprint drops the project's entries, the read that saw the change not storing its answer either. TestCacheDropsWithAPolicy caches a read, drops the policy, lets the check fall due, and gets the empty answer, with the old entry gone.

    Writes and functions#

    write and batch run in the caller's transaction (inTx), so policies' USING and WITH CHECK apply. An *apiError anywhere rolls the whole transaction back.

    • Insert: one row or up to 1,000, through json_populate_recordset(NULL::table, $1) naming only the columns sent, so defaults fill the rest and Postgres does the types (insert). on_conflict=cols makes it an upsert: DO UPDATE SET the sent columns, or DO NOTHING with resolution=ignore.
    • Update and delete need a key or a filter (400 filter_required, target). They run first and count afterwards. Above max_affected (1,000 by default, at most 100,000) the transaction rolls back with 400 too_many_rows.
    • Batch: up to 50 operations in one transaction. The first failure rolls back everything and names its index in details.operation.
    • Idempotency-Key (idempotencyOf): the key is claimed by xb_auth.idempotency_claim inside the write's own transaction, scoped to role:sub. A repeat within 24 hours gets the first answer, and the same key with a different request gets 422. Without a user or the secret key it is refused, because every anonymous caller would share one scope.
    Resolved

    return=minimal used to ask for the rows back anyway: every write's CTE ended RETURNING *, and Postgres applies the table's SELECT policies and column privileges to returned rows, so a table anon may insert into but not read (a contact form, a waitlist, an event log) refused every insert with 403 permission_denied. Now a minimal insert, update or delete runs without RETURNING (returning passes the statement through) and runWrite takes affected from the command tag, so max_affected still applies. An upsert still needs SELECT, because Postgres checks the SELECT policies of a row an ON CONFLICT insert writes. TestMinimalWritesNeedNoSelect inserts one row, two and a batch under an INSERT-only policy, and counts minimal updates and deletes.

    Functions (rpc) take named arguments only. pickFunction chooses the overload whose names cover the arguments sent and that gets every argument without a default, and answers ambiguous_function rather than guess. Each argument is a parameter cast to its declared type (argValue; arrays come as JSON arrays). GET is allowed for STABLE and IMMUTABLE functions only (405 volatile_function), so a link or a prefetch never changes data, and only such calls are cached. Set-returning functions take select, where, order and limit on their output, by treating it as a view, and the whole call goes through the cost guard. The call runs with the caller's EXECUTE privilege, after the function gate for anon and user. A SECURITY DEFINER function runs as its owner, which the advisor flags.

    The visual schema editor#

    The table editor's schema changes are built by schemaedit.Build, a pure function from a Change and a State to a Plan: statements, risk notes, a reverse migration, a slug and a hash. gatherState fills the state from the database, with parameters throughout: size and row estimate, the column's current type, nullability and default, whether a type change rewrites (rewrites: same type with a wider modifier, or a binary-coercible cast, does not), whether a default is volatile, and the definition of what is dropped.

    • Names are always quoted (Ident), at most 63 bytes. Types must match typeRe (identifiers, an optional schema, modifiers of digits, []) and exist (to_regtype). Expressions (defaults, checks, USING, index predicates) go in as written, which is the point. They run as the project's owner, who could run them in the SQL console anyway, and ApplySchema sends each statement with ExecParams, so one cannot carry a second.
    • Risk notes carry info, warning or danger, and rise to danger past 100 MB. They cover rewrites, volatile defaults, NOT NULL without a default on a table with rows, constraint checks under lock (offering NOT VALID), SET NOT NULL's scan, and drops. Indexes are built CONCURRENTLY by default.
    • Reverse migrations are written where they are unambiguous (a rename back, a drop of what was added, the old default or type, the old constraint or index definition), and as DownTODO notes where they are not (data that is gone, an enum value Postgres cannot remove). Render writes plain SQL, goose or dbmate, marking non-transactional plans.
    • A batch (the "Edit table" panel) is up to 100 transactional changes to one table, with a rename last.

    Who may run what. Preview and migration export need project.console_read. Applying needs project.table_edit, developer and up, with token scope write, and the admin scope for a token whose plan drops something (ApplySchemaChange). ApplySchema refuses a project whose console is read-only, rebuilds the plan on the owner's session, and runs it only if its hash still matches the preview (ErrStalePlan). A drop also needs the dropped object's name typed. It runs with a 5-second lock timeout and a 10-minute statement timeout, and the audit log records the SQL.

    Typed definitions#

    typegen.Generate renders the catalog, read as the platform (Service.Types, GET …/services/types, xenibase gen types), as TypeScript (a Database interface shaped like Supabase's, with Row, Insert and Update, views and functions), Dart (classes with fromJson and toJson) or Go (a struct per relation, plus Insert and Update structs with pointers where a field may be left out). A column is optional on insert when it is nullable or has a default. Generated columns are left out of inserts and updates.

    Names are data, never source. They reach a file only as string literals, escaped for the language (strconv.Quote for Go, JSON's escaping for TypeScript, dartString for Dart, which also escapes $), or in comments, quoted when a character does not print. Identifiers are made by camel from letters and digits only (ASCII ones for Dart and TypeScript), start with a letter, and are numbered by a namer when two come out the same or meet a reserved word or a name the file uses (class_, List2). A Go JSON tag can hold only what encoding/json accepts, so a column with any other character is refused for Go with an error naming it, which the API answers as 400; TypeScript and Dart take any name.

    Resolved

    Generated code used to take database names as source text. Go field names only lost _ - . space, the update tag held the raw name in a backquoted string, and comments and Dart's json['…'] took names as they were, so a column named x⇥int⏎}⏎func⇥init()⇥{⇥panic("ran")⏎// (37 bytes) put init functions into every program built with the generated package, and a $ or ' broke the Dart file. Now names appear only escaped in strings and comments, identifiers are built from letters and digits, and a column Go cannot tag is refused. TestNamesAreNotCode uses the 37-byte name as a table and a column: Go refuses the column and, for the table, parses and type-checks with no function declared; the TypeScript and Dart files have the same lines as with a plain name, with the name only in escaped literals.

    Failure handling#

    What failsWhat happens
    enable_services fails at roles, schema or keyRetried, three attempts in all. Every step can run again. Services stay off and the keys made at the request stay unused until it succeeds.
    A schema version failsThat version's transaction rolls back and the recorded version stays lower. The reconciler tries again every 15 s and logs a warning per project.
    Exposing a schema that does not exist, or a forbidden name400 from validExposure or applyExposure. Nothing is stored.
    The project moves, is restored or a branch is resetThe reconciler repairs roles, takes the xb_* objects back, re-runs every version and the exposure grants. Requests in between may fail on missing grants.
    A table or column the cached catalog lacksThe fingerprint catches it within 2 s. A 42P01 or 42703 drops the catalog at once. The request answers 404 unknown_table or 400 unknown_column.
    The edge's sync_grants fails, or the project is behind version 7Logged (a missing function quietly). The request goes on: the gates still refuse unprotected relations, views over them, and invoker functions to a role that reaches one, with 403 rls_required. The next catalog change tries again, and the reconciler brings the version.
    A query over the cost limit400 query_too_expensive with the estimate and the limit. Nothing ran.
    The statement timeout504 statement_timeout. The transaction rolls back. An exact count that times out answers count: null instead.
    A write over max_affected, or a batch operation failingThe whole transaction rolls back: 400 too_many_rows, or the operation's error with its index.
    An Idempotency-Key on a project behind version 6503 idempotency_unavailable with Retry-After: 60 until the reconciler catches up.
    A write commits but the answer is lostWithout a key, a retry writes again. With a key, the retry gets the stored answer.
    The database is unreachable or paused503 database_unavailable. A paused project is woken (the waker).
    A schema change whose preview is staleErrStalePlan: preview again. A failing statement returns DDLError with the statement. A transactional plan rolls back, but a concurrent index build that fails leaves an invalid index to drop.
    Spec and code differ

    V4 §2.3 has the edge login SET ROLE to the three request roles. Each request role is now a login of its own, and the edge login holds no memberships (V4-M32 #18). §3.1 refreshes the catalog through an event trigger that bumps a schema version. The edge polls a fingerprint every 2 seconds instead, because only a superuser can create an event trigger and owner-run restores would fail on one (V4-M29 #1). §3.6 refuses queries above "the plan's limit", cached "per normalised query shape". The limit is a project setting, the same 1,000,000 on every plan, and nothing is cached: a plan kept per shape let one request's values vouch for another's (see How a request runs). §3.8 drops cached entries "via the same schema-version and change signals realtime uses". Writes through the same edge drop them, realtime does so only on edges with subscribers, and a schema, policy or privilege change drops all of them within 2 seconds. Other data changes show within the TTL. §3.6 says column privileges are respected: they are, but select=* then fails rather than leaving the column out, and hiding a column takes the table-level grant away first (the RLS gate). docs/backend-services.md says a write's select takes no relations, but returning passes them to the read builder, gated like reads.
