    • projauth1,223 linesThe auth data of a project (V4 §4.2): users, sessions, rotating refresh tokens, one-time codes and the audit log in the project's xb_auth schema. xenibase-edge serves auth through it, as the project's edge login; xenibase-server's dashbo…
    • jwtes203 linesSigns and verifies ES256 JSON Web Tokens and handles their public keys as JWKs (V4 §4.4).
    • messaging538 linesSends one-time codes by SMS and WhatsApp (V4 §4.6): phone numbers normalised to E.164, the country they belong to, and the providers Xenibase or a project sends through (Termii, the WhatsApp Business Platform's Cloud API, Twilio, Africa's …
    • totp91 linesRFC 6238 one-time codes, shared by operator accounts and project users' second factors (V4 §4.1).

    Who does what#

    projauth does every read and write of xb_auth, on the caller's transaction. The edge's routes (edge.auth and the files beside it) run each request as one transaction as the project's edge login (withAuth), the only login with rights on those tables. xenibase-server renders and queues messages and hooks (authmessage.go, authhook.go), and holds the settings, sealed secrets and signing keys (authconfig.go) that reach the edge on the signed feed (The data API).

    The xb_auth data#

    Schema versions 2 and 3 in services/schema.go create the tables; version 10 adds to them. Request roles see only xb_auth.user_profiles, with no hashes, tokens or factors: a user sees their own row, the service role and the owner every row, anon nothing.

    TableHoldsNotes
    usersEmail and phone (each unique when set), the argon2id or bcrypt hash, confirmation times, app_metadata, user_metadata, banned_until, failed_sign_ins, locked_untilEmails lowercased and trimmed; phones E.164.
    identitiesOne row per way in: email, phone or an OAuth provider, unique on (provider, provider_id)EnsureIdentity upserts and reports ErrExists when another user holds it.
    sessionsA signed-in device: aal, amr (methods with times), user agent, IP, refreshed_at, not_afterCascades to its refresh tokens.
    refresh_tokensSHA-256 of a 256-bit random token, its session, its parent, revokedSingle use (below).
    one_time_codesOne row per code: kind, target (address or number), the code's hash salted with the row id, the link token's hash, attempts, expires_at, and password_sha, a hash of the password hash the request that sent it setA new code of a kind replaces the user's earlier one (NewCode).
    flow_stateAn OAuth sign-in in progress: state hash, the edge's PKCE verifier to the provider, nonce, the app's challenge, redirect, then the app's one-time code hashRows an hour past expiry are deleted at each new /authorize.
    mfa_factors, mfa_challengesTOTP secrets (in clear, base32) and phone numbers, with failed_attempts and locked_until; challenges with a code hash, attempts, verified_atAt most 10 factors a user (MaxFactors).
    code_requestsEach request for an email or phone code: a hash of the address or number, the kind, the timeRecorded whether or not the target has a user; rows over a day old are deleted a few at a time as new ones come (RecordCodeRequest).
    audit_logAction, user, IP, detailsThe actions are the Act… constants in projauth. Nothing prunes it.

    TOTP secrets are in clear, so whoever reads the database as its admin, or a decrypted backup (Backups, restores and imports), can compute every user's second factor.

    Passwords#

    signup checks the address, passwordProblem (at least password_min_length characters, 8 by default, at most 256 bytes refused rather than cut, optionally letters and digits) and the redirect, and hashes before opening the transaction. Hashing is argon2id at OWASP's minimum (19 MiB, 2 passes, 1 lane), because one edge hashes for every project in its region. Hashes take one of as many slots as the edge has CPUs (hash).

    • Confirmation on (the default): a new user is created unconfirmed and sent a code and link. The answer is {"confirmation_sent": true} whether the address was new, unconfirmed or confirmed, so sign-up does not reveal who has an account (M31 #6).
    • Confirmation off: the user is signed in at once, and a taken address answers 422 user_already_exists, as Supabase does. The security review accepts this.

    signinPassword locks the user's row, refuses a locked user, and checks the password with CheckPassword, which hashes against a fixed dummy hash when there is no user, so a missing user costs the same as a wrong password. A wrong password counts in RecordFailedSignIn: from the fifth in a row the user is locked for a minute, doubling with each further failure up to a day. A success clears the count. A bcrypt hash brought from Supabase is accepted and replaced with argon2id in the same transaction (Rehash, conditional on the old hash).

    The lockout is per user, not per client, so anyone who knows an address can lock its owner out of password sign-in with about fifteen wrong guesses spread over a few minutes, for most of a day. Magic links and OAuth still work.

    A squatter can sign up first with someone else's address and a password of their own. While the account is unconfirmed the squatter cannot sign in. A sign-up for an address whose row is still unconfirmed replaces the row's password with the new request's and ends its sessions. Each code records the password its request set (NewPasswordCode; a code sent again by /resend keeps the one it replaces). useVerified clears the password when a magic link or recovery code first proves the address (M31 #12), and when a signup or invite code does and the password is not the one its request set (KeepsPassword):

    Resolved

    A squatter used to keep their password through the owner's own sign-up: signup found the unconfirmed row and only sent a new code, dropping the owner's password, and useVerified cleared passwords only for magiclink and recovery. Admin-API invitations (linkFor reused the row) and phone sign-up (signupPhone) did the same. Now a sign-up again for an unconfirmed address or number, or a sign-up link from the admin API with a password, replaces the password and ends the row's sessions, and its code records that password. A signup, invite or phone_signup code that first proves the address or number clears any other password and ends the sessions (usePhoneVerified for numbers). A squatter who signs up again after the owner therefore leaves the owner's code with no password rather than theirs. TestSquatterLosesPasswordToOwnersSignup covers each path.

    A new password through PUT /auth/v1/user (updateUser) ends every other session of the user (ASVS 3.3.3, V4.1-M11 #4). It does not ask for the current password. A user with a verified factor needs an aal2 session to change the password or email (MFA). A password set through the admin API or the dashboard ends no sessions.

    Email links and codes#

    Every email carries a 6-digit code and a link token, made by NewCode from crypto/rand. Both last 10 minutes; an invitation lasts 24 hours. Only hashes are kept. The kinds are signup, magiclink, recovery, invite and email_change.

    • Code. POST /verify with email and token goes to VerifyCode. It takes the newest unexpired code of the allowed kinds for that target, under a row lock. A wrong code adds one to attempts. After five, the code is refused even when right, until it expires or a new code replaces it, which the one-a-minute rule holds back (V4.1-M11 #2).
    • Link. GET /verify?token=…&type=… needs no API key, since it is clicked from a mail client (keylessAuth). VerifyToken deletes the row by the token's hash. verifyLink redirects with the session in the URL fragment, never the query, with Referrer-Policy: no-referrer. Without a redirect it shows a plain page.
    • One a minute. tooSoon refuses a code for an address within 60 seconds of the last request for one of the same kinds, counting requests in code_requests (RecentCodeRequests, under an advisory lock per address) whether or not the address has a user. It also refuses a sixth code of any kind to an address within an hour and a twenty-first within a day (emailsPerHour, emailsPerDay), with Retry-After until the oldest leaves the window.

    The edge asks xenibase-server for the email inside its transaction (sendEmail), so a refusal rolls the code back. queueEmail renders the project's template (the default if it fails on real data), seals and queues it. A worker sends through the project's SMTP, or the platform's at 30 an hour per project (PlatformEmailsPerHour), with five tries.

    Redirects are checked by redirectAllowed: the site URL's scheme and host with its path or one below it, or an exact entry of redirect_urls, or, when allow_wildcard_redirects is on, a pattern. patternAllows matches a pattern against the parsed URL part by part: the scheme exactly, the host label by label with * inside one label (hostMatch), the port exactly or * for any, and the path with * matching anything but / and ** anything (globMatch). A query or fragment passes only a pattern with a matching one or a path ending in **. URLs with a user part are refused.

    Resolved

    Wildcard redirects used to match the whole URL as text, so they allowed other hosts: globMatch ran the pattern over the raw string, where * also matched ? and #, and with https://*.example.com/** the URLs https://evil.test?.example.com/ and https://evil.test#.example.com/x passed, sending a magic link's tokens to evil.test. Now the candidate is parsed first and patternAllows compares scheme, host, port and path separately, the host by its labels, so * stands for one label (or part of one) and never reaches the query or fragment. TestRedirectPatternsMatchHostAndPathApart covers these URLs and others.

    recover and resend answer {"sent": true} whether or not the address has a user, as M31 #6 intends, and so does their rate check.

    Resolved

    The one-a-minute check used to reveal which addresses have users: tooSoon counted codes for the address, and only a real user gets a code, so two POST /recover calls answered 200 then 429 over_email_send_rate_limit for a known address and 200 twice for an unknown one, and signin/otp without user creation did the same for addresses and numbers. Now every request for a code is recorded in xb_auth.code_requests (schema version 10) before the user is looked up, and the rule counts requests, so both kinds of address get 200 then 429. TestCodeLimitsDontRevealUsers covers recovery, email and phone sign-in codes and /resend.

    Anonymous sign-in (signinAnonymous, a sign-up with no credentials, off by default) makes a user with is_anonymous. Confirming an email or phone change, or linking a provider, makes it permanent. An email change sends a code to the new address only. The old address is not asked.

    Phone codes by SMS and WhatsApp#

    messaging.Normalize makes E.164 (08031234567 becomes +2348031234567; other countries need + or 00), and Country maps the calling code to a country (the largest for shared codes such as +1). The edge (countryAllowed) and xenibase-server both check it against the project's list.

    Phone codes are the same one_time_codes rows, with kinds phone (sign-in), phone_signup and phone_change, and the same five tries. signinPhoneOTP creates the user when sign-ups allow it and answers the same either way. The edge allows one code request a minute per number, counted whether or not the number has a user (phoneTooSoon). xenibase-server applies the rest in queuePhone, under a per-project advisory lock so counts hold across edges:

    ControlValueWhere
    CountriesNigeria unless the project lists othersphone_countries
    Per numberOne a minute (edge), five an hour (server)PerNumberPerHour
    Per projectphone_daily_cap, 200 by default, 1 to 100,000; through the platform's providers also the plan's sms_codes_per_day (planSMSCap), the lower winningDefaultPhoneDailyCap
    AlertsProject admins emailed once a day when the cap is hit and when a quarter of it goes in an houralert
    Free plansWith DisallowFreePlans, a Free organisation must bring its own providerqueuePhone

    A refusal comes back to the edge as a status, which sendPhone turns into 429 over_sms_send_rate_limit, 403 phone_not_allowed or 503 sms_send_failed, and the code is rolled back. The worker (sendOne) sends by one of three routes:

    • The platform's providers: Termii over its DND route for SMS (it reaches numbers registered as do-not-disturb), Africa's Talking as fallback, and the WhatsApp Cloud API. Each message is metered with its cost (meterMessage, Billing, Free tier and capacity).
    • The project's own provider: Termii, Africa's Talking, Twilio or the WhatsApp Cloud API, credentials sealed at xenibase-server (provider). A base_url is reached only through the outbound rules (providerClient): a public address or an allow-listed host, connected to at the address checked, with no redirects followed.
    • The send-message hook: when send_message_url is set, every email and code goes to it as a signed webhook instead (sendMessageHook).
    Resolved

    The project's SMTP host and provider base URL used to bypass the outbound rules that hooks go through: mail.Config.Validate took any host and port, PhoneProvider.validate any https base_url, xenibase-server dialled them directly, and the SMTP test's 502 carried the dial error, so a project admin could map the control plane's network or have the worker POST to an internal service. Now pinSMTP checks the SMTP host with outbound.CheckAddr (public addresses only unless the platform admin allow-listed the host, never link-local or metadata) and the connection goes to the address checked (mail.Config.DialAddr); a provider's base_url passes outbound.Check and is called with a client pinned the same way. TestAuthSMTP answers 400 for a refused address and a generic 502 for any other failure, whose detail goes only to the log. TestProjectSMTPAndProviderGoThroughOutbound and TestCheckAddr cover it.

    OAuth providers#

    Each project uses its own app at Google, Apple, GitHub, Facebook or Microsoft (oauthProviders). Secrets travel sealed on the feed, and Apple's client secret is an ES256 JWT the edge signs (appleSecret).

    1. Authorize. oauthAuthorize (no API key, the sign-in rate) checks the redirect, takes the app's PKCE challenge (S256 by default, or plain, 43 to 128 characters), and stores a 10-minute flow_state row with the state's hash, the edge's own PKCE verifier to the provider, a nonce and the redirect.
    2. Callback. callback (GET, or Apple's form POST) uses the state once, by overwriting its hash, then exchanges the provider's code itself (providerUser). ID tokens from the token endpoint are trusted over TLS, as OIDC Core §3.1.3.7 allows, after idTokenClaims checks audience, expiry and nonce.
    3. Hand-off. With a challenge, the app gets a one-time code in the query (5 minutes), which exchangePKCE trades with the verifier at token?grant_type=pkce. The row is deleted before the verifier is compared, so a wrong verifier burns the code. Without a challenge, the session goes in the fragment (the implicit flow).

    oauthUser picks the user in this order: the identity's owner; the signed-in user linking it (/user/identities/authorize, when manual_linking is on); a user with the same address if the provider says it is verified; or a new user. An email the provider does not mark verified never links. Microsoft's counts as unverified, which closes the nOAuth class of takeovers, and Facebook's counts as verified. Joining an unconfirmed user by a verified email clears its password and ends its sessions, as magic links do. UnlinkIdentity refuses a user's last identity. Unlinking the email or phone identity also clears that column.

    Note

    The state is tied to its flow_state row, not to a browser: the edge sets no cookies. With PKCE the app's verifier covers that. Without it (the implicit flow, or a link flow), a provider URL started by one person and finished by another completes the first person's flow.

    MFA#

    Second factors are TOTP apps and, when mfa_phone is on, phone codes. The policy is off, optional (the default), required, or claim (required for users whose app_metadata.mfa_required is true). The gateway applies it to data and realtime requests:

    • Enrol. mfaEnroll adds an unverified factor (Enroll); TOTP returns a 160-bit secret and its otpauth:// URI once. A user who has a verified factor enrols another only from an aal2 session (belowMFA, which requires aal2 both in the stored session and in the request's token); below it the answer is 403 insufficient_aal.
    • Challenge. mfaChallenge makes a challenge good for 5 minutes. A phone factor is sent a 6-digit code, at most every 30 seconds per factor (challengeEvery), under the same server caps as sign-in codes. A TOTP challenge has no limit.
    • Verify. VerifyChallenge allows five wrong tries per challenge. Wrong codes also count on the factor across its challenges: from the fifth in a row (FactorLockoutAfter) the factor is locked for a minute, doubling with each further one up to a day, and both its challenges and its codes answer 429 mfa_factor_locked with Retry-After (factorLocked). A right code clears the count. A TOTP code is checked one 30-second step either side (totp.Verify), and its step must be later than the factor's last_used_step, so a code works once. An unverified factor can be verified only when the user has no verified one or the session is at aal2 already. A right code verifies the factor, and StepUp raises the session to aal2 and appends to amr. The session's refresh tokens are replaced and new tokens issued.
    • Remove. mfaUnenroll needs aal2 to remove a verified factor. When none is left, LowerSessions drops the user's sessions to aal1.
    Resolved

    A session at aal1 used to be able to enrol a new factor and so reach aal2: mfaEnroll checked only that the session was alive, and mfaVerify raised the session on any factor of the user, so a password or a recovery link was enough to pass mfa_required. updateUser likewise changed the password or email at aal1. Now, when the user has a verified factor and the session (both as stored and as the token says: the session catches one lowered since, the token one issued before the step-up) is below aal2, enrolment answers 403 insufficient_aal, a password or email change 401 insufficient_aal, and so does verifying a factor enrolled before the user's first one was verified, as GoTrue does. A user's first factor still raises the session that verifies it. TestAAL1CannotChangeWhatProvesTheUser covers each.

    Resolved

    TOTP guesses used to be limited only by the project's request rate: five wrong tries used up a challenge, but a new one could be had at once, the /factors and /mfa/ routes had no auth rate group, and nothing counted failures per factor, so the gateway's 12,000 requests a minute per key found a code in under an hour. Now those routes are in the mfa group (30 a minute per IP), /user and sign-out in user (60), and five wrong codes in a row on a factor, across challenges, lock it for a minute, doubling up to a day, which leaves a few dozen guesses a day. TestTOTPGuessesLockTheFactor covers the lockout and both groups.

    Captcha and hooks#

    captcha runs when the project turned captcha on and stored its secret. It checks Cloudflare Turnstile's token, from gotrue_meta_security.captcha_token or captcha_token, on sign-up, password sign-in and code requests (M32 #14), with a 5-second limit. If Turnstile cannot be reached, the answer is 503 captcha_unavailable (fail closed). /recover, /resend and MFA challenges have no captcha.

    HookAsRunsOn failure
    Custom claimsA Postgres function schema.name(jsonb)At every token issue, in its own transaction as <db>_auth_hook, 2-second statement timeout, at most 16 KB back (runPGHook)The sign-in fails. Claims the edge sets cannot be changed (protectedClaims).
    Before sign-upA Postgres function, or a webhookBefore the user row (beforeSignup). The webhook is asked at once with a 3-second limit (beforeSignupTimeout)A function's error fails the sign-up. A webhook that errs, times out or answers 5xx lets it through (fail open, M32 #13).
    After sign-up, after sign-inWebhooksSent by the edge after the auth transaction commits (authTx), queued in auth_hook_outbox, delivered up to 8 times with backoff from 15 seconds (sendAuthHooks), kept 14 daysAn event the edge cannot hand over is logged and lost.
    Send messageA webhookFor every email and code, instead of sending (above)Retried with the message queue, five times.

    Webhooks go through the outbound client (Database webhooks and scheduled jobs), which refuses private addresses, applies the organisation's outbound limits and signs the body with the project's whsec_ secret in Xenibase-Signature. The secret is made when the first hook URL is set, and only project admins are shown it (hookSecretOut). decision reads the before-sign-up answer:

    Resolved

    Developers used to be able to read the hook signing secret: GET /api/v1/projects/{id}/auth/config needs only project.services_logs, the developer role (routeRules), and its answer carried the whsec_ secret in full, so a developer or a read token could forge hook events the project's servers trust. Now hookSecretOut includes the secret only when the caller may also do project.services (a project admin, with an admin token); everyone else gets hook_secret_set, and the dashboard shows "Set". TestHookSecretOnlyForProjectAdmins covers both roles.

    Sessions and refresh tokens#

    startSession is the one way in: the MAU check, other sessions ended under single_session, the session and its first refresh token (NewSession, not_after from session_max_seconds), the audit entry, the after-sign-in hook, the access token.

    Row locks serialise two refreshes with one token, and the second ends the session: the theft detection (refresh_token_reused, audited). With no grace period, a client that refreshes twice at once, such as two tabs, signs itself out too. session_inactivity_seconds (0 by default, otherwise at least 600) ends a session not refreshed for that long. Sign-out (signout) deletes the session (local), all of them (global) or the others. A ban refuses sign-in and the next refresh but deletes no session (M31 #10). Admin sign-out ends them all.

    Routes under /auth/v1/ that act for the user read the session first (liveUser), so an ended session's token fails there. The data API, storage and realtime only verify the token, so it works there until it expires.

    Spec and code differ

    docs/security-review.md (ASVS 3.3.1) says "ended sessions' access tokens are refused at once (the edge checks the session), not at expiry". That holds for /auth/v1 only. After sign-out, a password change, reuse detection or a ban, a stolen access token keeps reading and writing data until its exp: an hour by default, up to a day. V4 §4.8 says the same thing the code does ("a short access-token lifetime bounds the window").

    Signing keys and tokens#

    Every project has its own P-256 key, made when backend services are turned on (ensureJWTKey). The private half is sealed under the master key with the row's id as associated data. A branch gets a new key, never its parent's (Database branches). The feed decrypts each live project's active key and sends it to the edges (feed), which sign tokens themselves (M31 #2). Every edge in a region therefore holds the private keys of every project there.

    • Lifetime. access_token_ttl, 3,600 seconds by default, 300 to 86,400. jwtes.Sign writes alg: ES256 and the key's kid.
    • Verifying. The gateway takes a Bearer token only with the publishable key (authorize). jwtes.Verify refuses any algorithm but ES256, finds the key by kid among this project's keys only, checks the signature, exp and nbf with a minute's leeway, and requires aud to be the project's ref. The gateway then requires role: user. A token from another project fails on both key and audience (FuzzGatewayIsolation).
    • JWKS. GET /auth/v1/.well-known/jwks.json (no key, cached 10 minutes, jwks) lists the active and verifying keys, so the project's own servers verify with no shared secret.
    • Rotation. RotateSigningKey (project admin) demotes the active key to verifying until 24 hours and 5 minutes from now, the longest possible lifetime plus skew, whatever the project's own TTL. It then inserts the new key. A trigger on project_jwt_keys puts the project back on the feed. The services loop retires lapsed keys (RetireJWTKeys), and they leave the JWKS and the edges.
    • Revocation. RevokeSigningKey (project admin, POST …/auth/signing-keys/{keyId}/revoke or the dashboard's Revoke) retires one key at once, for a key that leaked. The trigger puts the project on the feed, so the key leaves the JWKS and the edges within seconds and every token it signed is refused. Revoking the active key inserts a new one in the same transaction, which signs every user out.
    Resolved

    A leaked signing key used to be impossible to withdraw at once: rotation was the only control, and it keeps the old public key verifying for 24 hours and 5 minutes, so after an edge compromise forged tokens stayed valid for a day. Now POST /api/v1/projects/{id}/auth/signing-keys/{keyId}/revoke (project.services) retires the key at once, and revoking the active one makes a new one. TestRevokeSigningKeyWithdrawsItAtOnce covers both, with the keys the feed then carries.

    Who in Xenibase sees a project's users#

    The dashboard reaches xb_auth through the management API, which connects to the project's database as the platform's admin (withProjectAuth). Actions are checked by authz.Can like every route (Security and tenant isolation).

    RouteActionRole, token scope
    GET …/auth/users, …/users/{userId}, …/auth/auditproject.auth_usersDeveloper, read
    POST …/auth/users, PATCH and DELETE …/users/{userId}, …/signoutproject.auth_users_manageDeveloper, write
    GET …/auth/config, …/auth/hooks, …/auth/signing-keysproject.services_logsDeveloper, read
    PATCH …/auth/config, SMTP test, template preview, key rotation and revocationproject.servicesProject admin, admin

    A user's detail shows identities, sessions and the last 50 audit entries; metadata, confirmation, bans, deletion and sign-out can be changed. Passwords are never shown, and set only when the dashboard creates a user. Changes are audited in xb_auth.audit_log as dashboard:<operator id> and in Xenibase's audit log. The project's servers do the same and more through the admin API with the secret key (admin), including links made without sending (generate-link).

    Rate limits#

    Auth requests pass the project's gateway limits first: per IP and per key, per minute, as token buckets with a sixth of a minute's burst (limiter.allow). A spend cap does not tighten them on /auth/ (V4 §12). authLimit then applies a bucket per group, project and IP:

    GroupPer IP a minuteRoutes
    signup10POST /signup (also anonymous and phone)
    signin30/signin/password, token?grant_type=password, /authorize
    otp10/signin/otp, /resend
    verify30/verify (both), /callback
    token120Refresh, the PKCE exchange
    recover10/recover
    admin600/admin/* (secret key)
    mfa30/factors, /mfa/*
    user60/user, /user/identities/*, /signout

    Buckets are per edge process, so several edges multiply them. Per identifier there are the one-a-minute rules, five emails an hour and twenty a day per address, five SMS an hour per number, five tries per code or challenge, the factor lockout, and the password lockout. The IP is the connection's, or the last X-Forwarded-For entry from a trusted proxy.

    Resolved

    Email codes used to have no cap per address beyond one a minute: with the project's own SMTP, a chosen address's sign-in code could take 7,200 guesses a day (about 0.7%), while phone numbers had the server's five an hour. Now tooSoon also caps an address at five codes an hour and twenty a day, every kind together, counted on requests whether or not the address has a user, which leaves at most 100 guesses a day. TestEmailCodesCappedPerAddress covers both caps for an address with a user and one without.

    Monthly active users#

    A user is active in a month when they sign in or refresh. The edge notes the pair (meter.activeUser) and sends it with its reports. recordActive inserts one auth_mau row per project, month and user, and adds one to the auth_mau usage metric only when the row is new, so MAU counts distinct users (M31 #9). The dashboard shows the month's count. Billing is on Billing, Free tier and capacity.

    When the organisation's plan has a MAU limit and it is used up, the plan-limits sweep sets mau_blocked on the feed. It also sends a Bloom filter of the month's counted users at 1% false positives (bloom.New), about 12 KB for 10,000 users. mauAllowed lets in users the filter may hold (bloom.Has), or users this edge process let in this month (up to 50,000 per project), and refuses others with 429 mau_limit_reached and Retry-After at the next month. A false positive lets a new user in. The overshoot is bounded by one sweep of traffic (V4.1 §3.2).

    Spec and code#

    Spec and code differ
    • V4 §4.1 allows "shared Xenibase dev credentials" for OAuth on Free. There are none: enabling a provider requires the project's own client id and secret (Validate).
    • V4 §4.8's leaked-password check and §4.5's bounce and complaint handling are not built. V4.1 §1.3 records both as deviations, and V4.1-M11 #9 accepts the password check as an ASVS gap.
    • V4 §4.6 puts captcha "on OTP requests". It covers signin/otp but not /resend, which also sends SMS and WhatsApp codes, nor phone MFA challenges.

    Failure handling#

    If this happensWhat Xenibase does
    The project has no signing key yet503 signing_key_unavailable with Retry-After: 5; the transaction rolls back
    The pooler drops the edge's connection before anything ranOne retry on a fresh connection (withAuth); otherwise 503 database_unavailable
    xenibase-server refuses or cannot queue an email or codeThe code is rolled back; 429 with the limit's message, 403 for a country or channel, 503 with no provider
    SMTP or a provider fails after queuingFive tries with backoff from 15 seconds, then a failed row in message_sends; the user asks again
    The project's daily SMS cap is reached429 over_sms_send_rate_limit until the 24-hour window clears; admins emailed once a day
    A custom-claims or Postgres before-sign-up hook errors or takes over 2 secondsThe sign-in or sign-up fails
    The before-sign-up webhook errs, times out (3 s) or answers 5xxThe sign-up goes through
    An after-sign-up or after-sign-in event cannot reach xenibase-serverLogged by the edge and lost; once queued, 8 deliveries with backoff, then failed
    Turnstile cannot be reached503 captcha_unavailable: the request is refused
    An OAuth provider's exchange failsThe browser goes back to the app with provider_exchange_failed; the state is already used, so the user starts again
    A refresh token is presented twiceThe session ends; 400 refresh_token_reused; token_reuse_detected audited
    The plan's MAU are used upCounted users carry on; new ones get 429 mau_limit_reached
    A signing key is rotatedOld tokens verify for 24 hours and 5 minutes; edges sign with the new key from their next feed read
    A signing key is revokedTokens it signed are refused from the edges' next feed read; revoking the active key signs every user out

    The request roles and the connections the edge makes for data requests are on The data API. The operator accounts' own sign-in, which shares internal/totp and internal/argonpw, is on Identity, organisations and access.

    Part D · Backend services

    File storage

    Buckets and objects for a project: the rules the edge and server share, signed URLs, uploads, image transforms in render workers, and the CDN.

    File storage is the third backend service (V4 §5). Buckets and objects are rows in the project's own database, in xb_storage, read and written as the caller's role, so the project's row-level security policies decide who may touch a file. The bytes are in the region's object store, under a key made from the object's version, which no caller chooses. xenibase-edge serves /storage/v1/ (storageRoute); xenibase-server runs the dashboard's storage, the sweep and the CDN purges.

    • files267 linesWhat xenibase-edge and xenibase-server share about backend services' storage (V4 §5): bucket and path rules, where an object's bytes are, the MIME checks, the signed URL tokens, and the SQL on xb_storage.
    • storage602 linesTalks to S3-compatible object storage (Cloudflare R2, Backblaze B2, MinIO, AWS) for backups (spec §3.2).
    • cdn64 linesPurges cached URLs from the CDN in front of xenibase-edge (V4 §5.4): a public bucket made private leaves the cache at once instead of after its max-age.

    Buckets, objects and versions#

    Schema version 4 of the xb_* schemas (schema.go, see Data API for how versions are applied) makes five tables, and version 8 a sixth, upload_tokens:

    TableHoldsWritten by
    bucketsId (the bucket rule, also as a CHECK), public, file_size_limit, allowed_mime_types, cache_seconds (0 to a year, default 3600)The edge's login (secret key only) and the dashboard. The owner and the service role may only read it.
    objectsBucket, path (1 to 1024 bytes), version (unique), size, MIME type, ETag, SHA-256 checksum, owner, user_metadata. UNIQUE (bucket, path).Callers as their role, under row-level security. Owned by the project's owner role, so developers write its policies in plain SQL.
    uploadsMultipart uploads in progress, with the starting caller's role and claimsThe edge's login
    upload_tokensSigned upload URLs not used yet, with the signer's role and claims, until they expireThe edge's login; a row goes when its URL is used, and the sweep removes expired ones
    garbageVersions no row points at any more, with when they were queuedThe trigger; emptied by the edge and the sweep
    usageOne row: total bytes and objectsThe trigger; corrected by the sweep

    A row names its bytes only through version, which the edge picks with uuid.New() for every upload. An overwrite is a new key and a row update, and a reader streaming the old version finishes, since old bytes stay for the garbage grace (a minute). A move changes only the row; a copy copies the bytes to a new version (decisions V4-M33 #2). One trigger keeps the queue and the totals:

    The trigger is SECURITY DEFINER and owned by the platform, so a policy or a request cannot forge the totals or the queue. A TRUNCATE by the owner fires no row trigger: the totals drift until the sweep recounts them, and the bytes are left to the reconciler (below). foldername, folder, filename and extension are helpers for policies, such as xb_storage.folder(path, 1) = xb_auth.uid()::text.

    Rules the edge and the server share#

    internal/files is imported by both binaries, so a bucket, path or token the dashboard makes is one the edge accepts:

    • Buckets. BucketRe: 1 to 63 lowercase letters, digits, _, . or -. ValidBucket also refuses, for new buckets, the ten words the routes use after /object/ and anything shaped like a UUID, so /upload/{id} never collides with /upload/{bucket}/….
    • Paths (ValidPath, below) are never part of a store key, so no path can reach another key.
    • Keys. Prefix is files/<ref>/, ObjectKey adds objects/<version>. A version is a uuid column, so even a row an owner writes by hand names a key in its own project's prefix.
    • SQL. InsertSQL (an upsert is ON CONFLICT … DO UPDATE, so an overwrite needs the UPDATE policy), ListFolderSQL (one folder level after a keyset cursor) and LikePrefix; plus the MIME checks and URL tokens below.

    TestPathsAndBuckets and the fuzz test in internal/files cover these; TestStorage sends %2e%2e, an empty segment and a NUL through the edge and gets 400 invalid_path.

    Who may read and write#

    A keyed request passes the key and JWT check (Project auth) and MFA if required. The edge then runs the statement the request implies on xb_storage.objects as the caller (decisions V4-M33 #4), inside asRole, whose objectsGate refuses anon and user with 403 rls_required while row-level security is off: the owner owns the table and could turn it off. With no policy, anon and user (NOBYPASSRLS) reach nothing and only the secret key's service role, which bypasses policies, reaches files. The edge's own login passes its own policy, xenibase_edge … USING (true), where the decision was made elsewhere:

    RequestKeyWhat decides
    GET /object/{bucket}/{path}, /object/info/…, /list/…, /render/{bucket}/… with a keyAnyThe SELECT policy, as the caller
    POST/PUT /object/…, /upload/…, /object/copyAnyINSERT (and UPDATE for an upsert), as the caller, checked before the bytes and again on commit
    POST /object/move, DELETE /object/…AnySELECT on the source, then UPDATE or DELETE as the caller
    /bucket…Secret onlyreq.Role == "service" in buckets
    GET /public/{bucket}/{path}, /object/public/…, /render/public/…, or /render/… without a keyNoneThe bucket's public flag, read by the edge's login; then any object in it
    GET /object/sign/…?token=, /render/sign/…, PUT /upload/sign/…NoneThe token; the policies were checked when it was made, and a signed upload is written as its signer, under the policies again

    keylessStorage answers the keyless rows before the key check, under the per-IP limit (storageRateOK), as billed requests. Anyone who can name an object in a public bucket can read it; listing still needs a policy. A private bucket answers 404 on the public routes. A policy's refusal is 403 not_allowed for a write and 404 for a read (storageError), so a reader cannot tell a hidden file from a missing one.

    The dashboard and xenibase storage act as the platform through /api/v1/projects/{id}/files…, with no policies but the same rules and a 50 MB upload cap (UploadFile, decisions V4-M33 #14), and download as a sandboxed attachment from the control plane's origin (DownloadStorageObject).

    Uploads#

    A direct upload (putObject) is POST (add X-Upsert: true to overwrite) or PUT (always upsert) to /object/{bucket}/{path}, with the bytes as the body or as the file part of a form, and optional metadata (a JSON object of at most 8 KB, plain or base64) in X-Metadata or a metadata part. In order:

    1. Bucket, read with the edge's login.
    2. Size. checkSize takes the smallest of 50 MB (directMax), the plan's largest upload and the bucket's file_size_limit. A known length over 50 MB but within the plan is told to use parts. With a quota, usage.bytes, the declared sizes of the large uploads in progress and the size must fit (413 quota_exceeded).
    3. Type. The first 512 bytes and the declared type go through DetectMIME, then the bucket's list (415 mime_not_allowed; entries are a type, type/* or */*).
    4. Policy, dry run. mayWrite runs the insert as the caller with a placeholder ETag and rolls it back, so no bytes are stored for a request the policies refuse.
    5. Bytes. A body of unknown length is first spooled to an unlinked temporary file, at most the limit plus one byte (spool). Then one PutObject of exactly that length, hashed with SHA-256 on the way.
    6. Row. commit inserts it as the caller, so the policies see the real size, type and metadata; on failure the new bytes are deleted.

    Large uploads (startUpload, V4 §5.3) go straight to the store. POST /upload/{bucket}/{path} with the size, type, upsert flag and metadata runs the same checks, starts a multipart upload, records an uploads row for 24 hours and returns presigned URLs for every part (at least 16 MiB each, at most 10,000 parts), each signed for exactly its part's length. The quota check and the row's insert run in one transaction holding the usage row, so uploads started together count each other, and a project may have 100 open (429 too_many_uploads). GET /upload/{id} lists the parts the store has and gives fresh URLs for the rest, so a failed part is sent again alone. POST /upload/{id}/complete (completeUpload) lists the parts at the store rather than trusting the client's ETags, requires parts 1 to n with exactly the declared total, completes, sniffs the first 512 bytes (deleting the object on a mismatch), and commits the row as the role and claims saved at the start. DELETE /upload/{id} aborts. The upload id is the only credential for these three.

    Resolved

    Parts used to be neither bounded nor counted until an upload completed: PresignPart signed the part number and upload id but no length, so each part URL took up to the store's part limit (5 GiB on S3 and R2) for 24 hours, and open uploads were not in the quota check, so uploads started together each passed against the same total. Now PresignPart signs Content-Length into each part's URL (the fixed part size, the last part the remainder), so the parts can hold no more than the declared size; checkSize (and the dashboard's upload) counts the declared sizes of the uploads in progress; startUpload checks the quota and records the row in one transaction that holds the usage row, so concurrent starts take turns; and a project may have maxOpenUploads (100) open (TestPresignedPartSignsItsLength, TestMultipartUploadsAreBoundedAndCounted). In-flight parts are still not in storage_gb_hours, but they are bounded by the declared size and the 24-hour expiry.

    Signed URLs#

    A signed URL lets someone without a key read one object, or upload to one path, until it expires (V4 §5.4, decisions V4-M33 #5). The token is a files.Token as base64url JSON (kind get or put, ref, bucket, path, expiry; optionally a download name, transform, upsert flag and owner, and for an upload the id of its upload_tokens row), a dot, and base64url of HMAC-SHA256 over "xenibase storage url\x00" and the payload. The key, storageSecret, is keyring.Derive("xenibase storage urls "+ref, 32), sent to the edge on the feed; it cannot be rotated per project, so only a new master key ends outstanding URLs.

    Made byChecked when madeLifetimeServed by
    POST /object/sign/{bucket}/{path} or /object/sign/{bucket} with up to 1000 paths (signDownload)The caller's SELECT policy finds the row; others get a per-path error1 hour by default, expires_in up to 7 daysGET /object/sign/… without a transform; with one, only /render/sign/…
    The dashboard (SignFile)The object existsThe sameGET /object/sign/…
    POST /object/upload/sign/{bucket}/{path} (signUpload)A dry-run insert as the caller, typed application/octet-stream, size 0; the caller's role and claims are saved in upload_tokens2 hours by default and at most; one uploadPUT/POST /upload/sign/…, token in the query or as a bearer

    signedDownload verifies the token and reads the row with the edge's login, so a URL keeps working after the signer loses access, until it expires. It names a path, not a version: an object replaced or re-created at that path is what it serves. A token for one project, bucket or path fails on any other (TestTokens, and TestStorage tampers with the path, the signature and the expiry).

    Resolved

    A signed thumbnail used to open the original: signDownload put the requested transform into an ordinary get token for a /render/sign/ URL, and neither Verify nor signedDownload looked at Transform, so the same token with render/sign changed to object/sign downloaded the full source. signedDownload now refuses a token that carries a transform (400 invalid_signature), as render already refused one without, so a signed preview serves only that render (TestSignedThumbnailDoesNotOpenTheOriginal).

    Resolved

    A signed upload URL used to skip the policies on what is written and could be spent many times: the policies saw only a placeholder row when it was made, signedUpload called putObject with no request so commit wrote the real row with the edge's login, which passes every policy, and nothing marked a token spent, so an upsert URL overwrote its path as often as its holder liked for up to 7 days. Now signUpload saves the caller's role and claims in a row of xb_storage.upload_tokens (schema version 8), named by the token's ID, and caps the URL at 2 hours. signedUpload uploads as that role and claims, so the dry run and the commit meet the policies with the real type, size and metadata (and an upsert asks UPDATE), and spendToken deletes the row in the edge's own transaction around the commit: only a write that commits spends the URL, and a second upload with it, on any edge, waits for the first and then finds it gone (400 invalid_signature). A token made before the upgrade has no row and is refused (TestSignedUploadIsTheSignersAndSingleUse).

    Downloads, ranges and cache headers#

    Every download path ends in serveObject. It answers 429 storage_egress_limit while the organisation's monthly download allowance is used up, then sets the headers:

    With nosniff also set, files are served from the project's API origin without running there: only PNG, JPEG, GIF, WebP, AVIF, BMP, video, audio, plain text and PDF are inline (inlineTypes); HTML, SVG and the rest are attachments. ?download forces an attachment, with that name unless it is 1 or true, percent-encoded into filename*. One range (bytes=a-b, a- or -n) is passed to the store and answered 206, or 416 outside the object; several or a malformed one get the whole object. If-None-Match on the store's ETag answers 304 before the store is asked. A served body counts as storage egress (meter.record).

    RouteCache-Control
    Public bucket, and its renderspublic, max-age= the bucket's cache_seconds
    Authenticated download or renderprivate, max-age= the bucket's cache_seconds
    Signed URLprivate, max-age= the seconds the token has left

    A shared cache stores only the public rows, and those are reachable without a key anyway, so a CDN in front of the edge cannot hand a private file to someone else.

    Image transforms#

    GET /render/{bucket}/{path}?width=&height=&resize=&format=&quality= resizes and converts PNG, JPEG, GIF, WebP and AVIF, as the caller's policies, a public bucket or a signed token allow (render, V4 §5.5), in pure Go: x/image scaling and WebAssembly builds of the WebP and AVIF codecs (decisions V4-M33 #8).

    LimitValueWhere
    Source size25 MB, from the row, and the read stops one byte past itrender, renderImage
    Source pixels25 million, from the header, before anything is decodedrenderBytes
    OutputUp to 2500 px a side; never scaled up; quality 20 to 100, 80 by defaultcheckTransform, resize
    Concurrent rendersHalf the edge's CPUs, at least one; a request waits for a slot until its deadlinerenderSlots in edge.New
    Time2 minutes per requestrender
    Monthly transformsNew renders refused with 429 transform_limit past the plan's allowance and 429 spend_cap_reached under a spend cap; cached ones still serveThe feed's TransformsBlocked, SpendCapped

    The decoder is picked from the magic bytes, not the stored type; a GIF becomes a PNG of its first frame. A render is stored at transforms/<version>/<hash>.<format>, hashed from transformKey, and answered X-Cache: MISS; repeats are read from there (HIT) without a slot. Only misses count toward image_transforms.

    Render workers (V4.1 §12.4, decisions V4.1-M11 #5). Unless XENIBASE_EDGE_RENDER_IN_PROCESS is set, each render runs in a child, xenibase-edge render-worker, one per slot, started on first use, with GOMEMLIMIT (XENIBASE_EDGE_RENDER_MEMORY_MB, 512 by default) and an RLIMIT_AS of 16 times that, since the WebAssembly runtimes reserve far more address space than they use (limitMemory). Requests and replies are length-prefixed frames on its stdin and stdout, a JSON header (at most 64 KiB) then the image (at most 26 MiB, readFrame).

    A worker does not recover panics: a decoder that panics or runs out of memory ends it, and the slot starts a fresh one next time (renderPool.render). TestRenderPool and TestRenderWorkerCrash crash one with a test marker while other renders carry on.

    A crash boundary, not a sandbox

    Workers run as the edge's user, with its file system and network, and inherit its whole environment (start), XENIBASE_EDGE_SECRET included. The decoders are memory-safe Go and WebAssembly, so an escape needs a bug there first; a minimal environment and a seccomp profile would be the cheap next steps.

    Where the bytes live#

    cmd/server sets services.Files to backup.FilesTarget: the region's files target (regions.files_target_id, a platform target, marked as in the region for a data-residency region), or, for a region without one, its backup target, the region's storage target or the platform default (decisions V4-M33 #1, Backups). Under it:

    KeyWhat
    files/<ref>/objects/<version>An object version's bytes, typed with its MIME type
    files/<ref>/transforms/<version>/<hash>.<format>Cached renders of that version
    projects/…, instances/…, metadata/…Backups, WAL-G archives and metadata backups, only in a region without a files target, where files share the backup target

    The target's own Prefix, if any, comes first (Target.Key). The edge gets the target, the project's prefix, the signing secret and its limits in storageConfig, and keeps one client per project while the target is unchanged. The ref is the services ref (8 characters, unique), not the project ID, and a branch has its own.

    Resolved

    Every edge used to hold the keys to the region's backups: the feed handed each edge the full storage.Target of the bucket that also holds the region's encrypted backups, WAL-G archives and metadata backups, kept apart only by the edge computing keys under files/<ref>/, so code running in the internet-facing edge, or a read of its memory, could delete every backup in the region. A region now takes a files target of its own (migration 00082, regions.files_target_id, Platform → Regions): a bucket for files, or the backup bucket with credentials scoped to files/ where the provider allows it. FilesTarget returns it to the feed and the sweep, so once it is set the feed never carries the backup target's secret; a deleted one fails rather than falling back. regions.Save refuses a files target that is any region's backup or copy target or the platform default, and DeleteTarget one a region's files are in. A region without one keeps its files in its backup target as before, so existing installs keep working: FilesTarget logs a warning (hourly per region) and the files_share_backups alert fires for each such region with storage (TestFilesTargetKeepsTheEdgesAwayFromBackups). Setting it doesn't move stored files: the operator copies files/ across first (docs/regions.md, "Files target").

    Resolved

    A region move used to leave every file behind: platform admins could move a non-residency project to another region's node, the move rewrote projects.region (moves.sql), the next feed pointed the edge at the new region's store, and nothing copied files/<ref>/, so every object answered "the object's data is missing" while the old bytes stayed unbilled. Copying the prefix as a move step would have to copy every version and render across stores and keep up with uploads during the move, so the move refuses instead: filesStay, called from checkMoveRegion when the move is asked for and again in runMove once writes are frozen for the cutover, answers 409 while xb_storage.objects or xb_storage.uploads has rows, naming the regions (TestRegionMoveRefusesAProjectWithFiles). A project with files must delete them, or be emptied and filled again after the move (docs/regions.md).

    The CDN and purges#

    The operator puts a CDN in front of the edges (decisions V4-M33 #11). With XENIBASE_CDN_CLOUDFLARE_* set, the server purges through cdn.Cloudflare, 30 URL prefixes a request, 15 seconds each (TestCloudflarePurge). A purge is due whenever files leave a public bucket's URLs: the bucket goes private, is deleted or emptied, or one of its objects is deleted, replaced or moved away. The edge's handlers send these as storage events in the background (storageEvent, three tries), and the dashboard's UpdateBucket, DeleteBucket, DeleteFiles and UploadFile purge directly. An object purges each public route's prefix up to its path, which covers its renders; more than 20 objects at once purge the whole bucket.

    Resolved

    A purge used to be tried once, and only when a bucket went private: if Cloudflare was slow or refused, the caller logged a warning and nothing retried, so the CDN could serve the now-private files for up to cache_seconds (a year at most), and deleting, overwriting or moving a public bucket's object, or deleting the bucket, purged nothing. Now every purge is a row in the metadata database's cdn_purges (migration 00083), tried at once by purge; one the CDN refuses stays, and RetryCDNPurges, part of every sweep, claims the due ones and tries them again after a minute, doubling to an hour, until the CDN takes them (rows older than a year, the longest cache time, are dropped). The events above cover deleted, replaced and moved objects and deleted or emptied buckets (TestCDNPurgesAreQueuedAndRetried, TestPublicFilesLeavingTheirURLsArePurged). An edge that cannot reach the server after three tries still only logs the event.

    The sweep, metering and clean-up#

    Deleted and replaced bytes go in two steps. The edge, a little after a write that queued garbage, removes queued versions older than the grace that no row names again, and their renders (collectSoon, collect). Anything it misses is left for xenibase-server, whose StorageSweep runs every 5 minutes on every server (services.Run) over the projects StorageProjects lists: schema 4 or later (services on, or turned off, which keeps the files), project active and not paused.

    1. Measure (sweepProject): sum xb_storage.objects as the admin, correct usage and record project_storage.
    2. Meter (meterStorage): set this hour's storage_gb_hours (a replace, so several servers meter once) for every live project in project_storage with files or renders, from its last measurement: the objects' bytes plus the renders' the reconciler measured, whether or not the sweep reached the project (paused, or its database down).
    3. Collect (collectGarbage): 200 queued versions at a time, FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, deleting the bytes and renders of those no row names. Then abort uploads whose row has expired.
    4. Limits (storageLimits): each project's quota is the organisation's file_storage_mb less what its other projects hold, plus upload_max_mb and the month's egress and transform flags, written only when they change, which moves the feed.
    5. Abandoned uploads (abandonedUploads): abort any multipart upload under files/ older than 25 hours, in each region's store.
    6. Deleted projects (cleanupDeleted): delete files/<ref>/ 30 days after deletion, with the final backup (ScheduleStorageCleanups).
    7. CDN purges (RetryCDNPurges): try again the purges the CDN has not taken (above).

    The reconciler, reconcileFiles, lists the prefix before reading the rows, so an upload finishing in between is not an orphan. It deletes bytes that no row, upload or queued removal names once 7 days old, and the renders of versions no row names; records rows without bytes for the storage page (decisions V4-M33 #12); and records what the kept renders take as project_storage.transform_bytes, which is metered with the files. It runs once a day across the servers: ReconcileStorageDue, on every pass of services.Run, claims the run in the one-row storage_reconciler table when the last is 24 hours old. TestStorageSweep covers the sweep, the reconciler and the purge.

    Resolved

    Some stored bytes used to go unmetered: storage_gb_hours summed objects.size over the projects StorageProjects listed, which left out projects whose backend services were turned off (Disable keeps every file, V4 §2.4), so an organisation could upload, turn services off and stop paying; and cached renders were never measured. Now StorageProjects lists a project whatever its services' state, metering is a pass of its own over every live project's last measurement (meterStorage), and the reconciler measures transforms/ into project_storage.transform_bytes (migration 00083), metered with the files (TestStorageIsMeteredWhateverTheServicesState, TestReconcilerMeasuresRenders). Renders made since the last reconcile are metered from the next, a day at most later; large uploads in progress are not metered, but are bounded by their declared size and the 24-hour expiry, and count against the quota.

    Resolved

    The reconciler used to run only after a server had been up for a day: services.Run kept its last run in a local variable, skipped the first chance and waited 24 hours from start, so servers deployed more often than daily never reconciled. The last run is now a row in the metadata database (storage_reconciler, migration 00083); ReconcileStorageDue claims it with one statement when it is 24 hours old, so exactly one server runs the reconciler each day, across restarts and deploys, and a new install runs it at once (TestReconcilerRunsNightlyAcrossRestarts). A server stopped mid-run leaves that day's run unfinished; the next is a day later.

    Backups hold rows, not bytes

    A restore brings back xb_storage rows, never bytes: files deleted since come back as rows without bytes, and files uploaded since lose their rows and go with the reconciler (decisions V4-M33 #13). A restore cannot undo deleting a file.

    Branches' files#

    A branch has its own ref, so its own prefix and signing secret, and its rows come with the data copy. With copy_files, copy_branch_files copies each version those rows name from the parent's prefix to the branch's inside the store; after a reset, strandedFiles first queues the branch's own bytes no refilled row names. Without it, the rows name bytes the branch lacks. Copies are the branch's objects, metered as such (Database branches).

    Failure handling#

    What failsWhat happens
    No object store for the region, or a client cannot be made503 storage_unavailable on every storage route
    The store errors on a read or write503 storage_unavailable, Retry-After: 5, logged; a deadline is 504
    The client's body ends early400 incomplete_body; nothing is committed
    The row's commit fails after the bytes are storedThe bytes are deleted (30 seconds, outliving the request); if that fails too, the reconciler removes them after 7 days
    A policy refusesWrites: 403 not_allowed, before any bytes; reads: 404
    Row-level security off on objects403 rls_required for anon and user; the secret key still works
    A row without bytes404 "the object's data is missing"; counted by the reconciler
    A multipart upload is never completedRow expired after 24 hours and aborted by the next sweep; any upload under files/ older than 25 hours aborted at the store
    A part sent with another length than its URL was signed forThe store refuses it (the signature covers Content-Length); the part's URL can be sent again with the right length
    A project already has 100 large uploads open429 too_many_uploads until some complete, are aborted or expire
    Complete with parts missing or the wrong total400 upload_incomplete; the upload stays open
    A render worker dies, or overruns 2 minutes500 transform_failed or 504 transform_timeout; a new worker next time (in process, a render runs to the end)
    Caching a render failsLogged; served, and rendered again next time
    The edge's clean-up failsLogged; the garbage stays queued for the sweep
    A project's database is unreachable in the sweepThat project is skipped and reported
    A CDN purge failsKept in cdn_purges and retried by the sweep, from a minute to an hourly backoff, until the CDN takes it (above)
    The edge cannot send a storage eventTried three times, then logged; that change is not purged
    A region move of a project with files409 when asked for; files uploaded during the move fail it at the cutover, before the region changes
    Deleting a deleted project's prefix failsRetried hourly, up to 50 attempts
    Spec and code differ

    Recorded in docs/decisions.md under V4-M33. V4 §5.1 stores objects at projects/<ref>/<bucket>/<path>; they are at files/<ref>/objects/<version>. §5.4 has signed URLs checked by "the object store or CDN" and Cloudflare "in front of R2"; the edge checks its own tokens and serves every byte, with any CDN in front of it. §5.5 names libvips and _transforms/; renders are pure Go under transforms/<version>/. §5.6 deletes a deleted project's objects; they go 30 days later.

    Spec and code differ

    Not recorded. Decisions V4-M33 #7 checks the declared type "any image for an image, text for text"; DetectMIME checks image, video and audio only, so any bytes may be declared text/html (the download headers keep that harmless). V4 §5.3's 24-hour abort happens at the next sweep, for the projects it lists, with a 25-hour store-wide pass behind it.

    Part D · Backend services

    Realtime

    Row changes and broadcasts to clients: the edge's realtime hub, its protocol, persisted topics, and the session-mode connection it listens on.

    Checked against bec3e57 · 2026-10-29
